subtopic: REPORTED IMPORTS FROM JAPAN THROUGH UNITED STATES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: REPORTED IMPORTS FROM JAPAN THROUGH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
On Wednesday, February 1, the hon. member for Lincoln asked a question with respect to the importation of electronic receiving tubes coming into Canada from Japan through San Francisco.
I am advised by my officers that inquiries have revealed that substantial quantities of Japanese electronic receiving tubes have been imported into Canada after transshipment at San Francisco. With two exceptions, in mid-November and early December, involving relatively small quantities, these tubes were imported prior to the imposition of the voluntary embargo by the Japanese. The importer concerned has followed the practice of placing the tubes in a bonded warehouse in Vancouver, to be drawn from stock as required.
All such tubes are being valued for duty at the fair market value prevailing at the time and place of transshipment to Canada. This means that the value for duty will be higher than the Japanese selling price by at least the amount of the United States duty and the shipping charges accruing from Japan to San Francisco.

speechtext:

subtopic: TORONTO
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INCLUSION OF SUBWAY IN FEDERAL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not agree with the description of any delegation from Toronto as high power in the sense that they endeavour to overpower in any way. A presentation was made by a delegation from metropolitan Toronto, headed by the metropolitan mayor and the mayor of Toronto, asking for consideration on the part of the government to the inclusion of their subway plan in the general scheme which is today the law of this country whereby the Department of Public Works makes available assistance in connection with pollution and the like.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 8, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. Flynn in the chair:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependants; to permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING PAYMENTS, PERMITTING APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to speak briefly this afternoon on the amendments to the Pension Act now before the house. Remarks have been made by many members about the excellent prospects envisaged by the resolution and the importance it will have to the some million and a quarter veterans throughout our country.
First of all, however, before discussing the measure I should like to congratulate the new Minister of Veterans Affairs. I think we all must pay tribute also to Colonel Brooks, the last minister, a member of the house for some 25 years, during whose period of approximately three and one half years as minister of the department many important changes and improvements were made.
The resolution before us at the moment is, I think, an excellent one, and comments to that effect have been made by officials of the Canadian Legion and other interested bodies across Canada. I should like to make some comments on the purposes of the legislation. Following upon its announcement in the speech from the throne, it is proposed by this legislation to increase the rate of pensions payable to disabled war veterans and to the dependants of those who lost their lives in the service of Canada. Incidentally, the number who lost their lives in the first and second world wars total some 104,000 Canadians. This, then, is one objective of the legislation.
Second, its purpose is to provide for increases in the maximum grants for burial expenses of pensioners. The amendment provides that the rates of such grants will keep

Pension Act
pace with similar payments for veterans who die in our treatment hospitals. The purposes and objectives of the legislation were outlined in some detail by the new Minister of Veterans Affairs on December 12, 1960 as found on pages 734 and 735 of Hansard.
A third aspect of the resolution deals with Canadian citizens who served in an allied force during either of the wars. It is proposed to bring in an amendment under which they may claim entitlement from the Canadian pension commission when their claims have been rejected by the government of the allied force in which they served.
Fourth, there are certain amendments which will affect payments to children. As the minister pointed out, the rates are to be increased. In addition there are certain technical changes involving the month in which a child becomes ineligible for such a pension during the sixteenth and seventeenth years. A further amendment will also provide for equalization of payments to all the children of a family rather than the present procedure whereby a greater amount is paid on behalf of the first child than on behalf of the second.
I am sure that these and other amendments will do much to bring a greater measure of fairness to this most important legislation. I am sure that some of the miscellaneous amendments and procedural changes in the Pension Act and its administration will also have a beneficial effect on our veterans and their dependants.
In this legislation we are concerned, of course, with our veterans. That goes without saying. Many members of our forces gave their lives and many others gave their health. In all cases they have given a considerable period of their lives to the protection of all of us here in Canada and, indeed, of the whole free world. The numbers of our Canadian veterans are very considerable. I mentioned earlier a million and a quarter people. The figures appear to indicate that from world war I we have some 240,000 survivors, and of this number approximately 49,000 are pensioners with disabilities exceeding 25 per cent. In the case of world war II the figure is 826,000 and the number of pensioners is some 100,000, or slightly over 12 per cent. To these pensioners we indeed owe a great deal. We cannot measure what we owe them, of course, in terms of dollars and cents, but we must try; and the process must be a continual one in order to bring about an increased measure of fairness in compensation to them for what they gave for us.
I thing we might look briefly at the past record. During the last three or four years the record has indeed been considerable. During Colonel Brooks' occupation of the

portfolio of veterans affairs some $47 J million was added by consent of the house to the amount being received by our veterans in disability pensions and war veterans allowances, and through increases to widows and dependant parents, educational assistance to children and increases for hospitals. This is indeed a considerable figure. Other things have been done as well. The resistance requirement for allied veterans was lowered from 20 to 10 years, and additional funds were made available for the Veterans' Land Act as well as in home construction loans for veterans. In summary, I think the record of the last three and a half or four years has been considerable and important.
One thing that strikes me about the many veterans in my riding, and I am sure this is true across the country, is that they continue to render service. Their service is not just in wartime. They appear to take part in virtually every community activity that goes on in my area, and I am sure that is true of other places across Canada.
I think it is important to know what our veterans are doing and not beside the point we are considering at the moment, because if we know what they are doing we will know better what they need and what their wishes and requests are, and I think that has an important relationship to this legislation. We have many important veterans organizations such as the Canadian Legion, the war amputation associations and various service associations across Canada. These and other organizations presented to the veterans affairs committee established in 1958, for which the government must be congratulated, briefs and important requests as to what should be done with respect to our veterans affairs legislation.
In my own country, for instance, there are some 2,000 to 3,000 members of the Canadian Legion. We have important and major branches of the Legion in towns such as Acton, Georgetown, Milton, Oakville and Burlington. In these communities our veterans, and our Legion members in particular, have made most important contributions. In my own home town of Georgetown they have recently contributed some $10,000 to the new hospital. In every community in my riding, and I am sure across Canada, they are most active in children's sports activities such as baseball and hockey. In my communities with a population of from 4,000 to 10,000 or more, one finds that 300 or 400 or more children each week are organized into sports activities by members of the Canadian Legion. In the town of Milton in my riding they take part in a portable hospital equipment campaign which makes equipment available to people in their homes.

A new Legion building in the town of Burlington in my riding has added much to that area. As an example of the community spirit and the continuing service which has been rendered by these veterans, I recall that two years ago when a school burned down in the town of Acton, a portion of the Canadian Legion building in that town was immediately turned over to the school children for their classes. Winter works projects are playing a part in the Legion activities, and funds have been contributed toward various such projects in my area. The veterans, acting through the Legion and working in community activities, are doing many things on a provincial and national basis. One example of this which comes to my mind is the eye bank. I believe also that about $75,000 or $80,000 has been paid out each year in scholarships to children going to universities in Ontario. These are some of the contributions they have made, Mr. Chairman.
What do our veterans ask of us in so far as this legislation is concerned, and perhaps with respect to future amendments or administrative changes? In talking to the veterans in my riding I note that the first thing they request is a substantial pension increase to disabled veterans. I should like to look briefly at a recent issue of the Legion magazine, the Legionary, for January, 1961, pages 4 and 7. We find that some of the financial problems facing our disabled veterans are outlined there. For instance, in the period from 1920 to 1957, and indeed until today, the annual pension of a 100 per cent disabled single pensioner has been increased from $900 a year to $1,800. The amount was doubled in that period of about 40 years.
If one compares that, as this issue of the Legionary does, with what they call a composite average wage from the year 1919 to 1958, one gets a different picture. This composite wage in 1919 was $900, about on a par with the pension granted at that time. The composite average wage in 1958 was $3,600, or four times the 1919 figure. While pensions have doubled during this time, we find that the composite average wage has been multiplied four times. I think this is a measure of the plight of some of our veterans. We are most pleased to see our government taking important action in this field.
It has been pointed out by several members during the last two days that section 70, the benefit of doubt section, as applied by our pension commission needs some attention. The Canadian Legion has indicated, and these figures must be available to all, that nearly 50 per cent of the cases heard on appeal during the year 1958-59 were successful. I feel that this rather extraordinary record points up the difficulty that there must be during the first hearing, and suggests that 90205-6-119
Pension Act
some change is needed. There should be a clearer interpretation of section 70 in order to give the veteran the benefit of the doubt. Indeed, I think the benefit of the doubt should not be interpreted in favour of the commission but must be given to the veteran himself.
It is not unnatural that in certain cases, perhaps judged on the medical evidence alone, some doubt would remain as to whether such injuries or complications resulted during wartime or before or after. In a field such as medicine this sort of doubt is only natural, and that such doubt should occur in a large number of cases is only natural. If we are putting the elimination of doubt on this basis of medical certainty, then it is only normal that a large number of cases will be turned down. However, if the veteran were given the benefit of the doubt I think we would reach a more equitable solution. This is one thing my Legion members are requesting.
The next request is for some change in the appeal board situation, perhaps in the way of balancing the composition of the board with a doctor, a lawyer and a layman. I believe this was the original intention. This point has been mentioned to me on numerous occasions. It may be that with such appeal boards the medical doubt takes precedence over the doubt that may exist in other parts of the case, particularly if there is more than one doctor. If the composition of such boards were changed somewhat it might be that a more realistic application of existing laws would be made.
These, Mr. Chairman, are the matters that have been brought to my attention by the veterans in my riding. They are delighted at the prospects for changes in this legislation, and we are indeed looking forward to the spelling out of the details regarding pensions and other matters in the immediate future.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to add a word before this resolution carries. I do not think anything needs to be added to the arguments or to the expressions of approval which have been given. I should like to say that in my own experience I think the Department of Veterans Affairs has shown the most admirable consideration for the veterans. I have always found that the pension advocates in particular really look after their clients as if they were being paid on the basis of the results.
I should also like to reiterate what has been said about the present minister and his predecessor, and to mention one or two names that I do not recall having been mentioned, inasmuch as we owe so much over many years to the men who have worked on these committees and have never relaxed their efforts to see that veterans were looked after. I refer to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the present lieutenant governor of British Columbia. Both of them, along with the others mentioned, devoted unceasing efforts to this cause.
Before I take my seat I should just like to add one slight bit of what I suppose might be called atmosphere. It might be of interest if it comes to the eyes of any of those who were around in August, 1914. It is extremely hard for people whose memory does not go back to that date to realize the feeling at that moment. I think there were two feelings. First of all there was the overwhelming feeling that war which up to that time in our memory had been rather a trivial thing-a brush on the northwest frontier of India- that lasted only a few days suddenly had become a real and terrible thing. But happily there were still those who could take it

lightly. You meet them in every army. I refer to people who do not take things too seriously.
I should like to put on record one case about which I know, that of a young man who joitfed up in August, 1914. I think his chief fear was that the war might not last long enough for him to get into it. That did not prove to be the case. In those days the pay was dished out in a rather informal manner. The paymaster just came around with a wad of bills and handed them out here and there. When handing them over to this young soldier he was surprised to hear him say, "What is that for?" The paymaster said, "That is your pay". "My God," said the young recruit, "do we get paid to fight?"
I like to think there were people like that around. They are needed to keep up the spirit of every army. I do not know about the career of that young man during the war. However, I am quite sure that he was a good soldier. Perhaps one could compare him with those who are mentioned in lines from Tennyson's "Ulysses":
-My mariners, . . .
That ever with a frolic welcome took
The thunder and the sunshine,-

Mr. Chairman, may I just wish the minister well in his new portfolio. I trust that he will show real initiative in the interests and the welfare of our veterans.
I congratulate the minister and the government on bringing in this resolution. Although we do not know the amount of the increases the bill will suggest, I hope they will be as generous as possible. Although this resolution covers only disability pensioners, I hope the minister will bring in a resolution dealing with the war veterans allowance, and that it will be on the same basis and effective at the same time as this legislation.
Many veterans on war veterans allowance find themselves in embarrassed circumstances today. With reference to the veterans of world war I who are now in the twilight of their lives and who spent one to four years in the mud and rat infested trenches in France and Belgium under heavy artillery fire, may I say this. Although they may not have been wounded, they suffered physical impairment which was indiscernible at that time. When hostilities ceased they were mentally upset, and by the time they got settled down or reestablished they ran into the years of the world-wide depression. Many had a difficult time in scraping out a bare existence. Others lost their savings and their insurance. Others ran into debt which took them years to pay off. Those were their most productive years and the years of their greatest earning power. Many of them never had a fair chance to provide for their declining years. I hope they will get the same treatment as those who were

on veterans pensions, the treatment they deserve. I repeat that I hope the minister brings in a duplicate resolution on war veterans allowance.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want briefly to add my voice to those who have spoken with approbation of this resolution and who look with anticipation to the legislation which will follow. I think it would be gilding the lily to say much more than has been said already. However, I feel that if I remained silent I would be derelict in my duty to my constituency, in which there was a tremendous record of enlistments during the early part of the war, in which there has been such a large percentage of veterans who have rehabilitated themselves, both those who were pensionable and those without pensions, and in which there is a tremendous interest in the Canadian Legion, which has many branches in all parts of the Peace river country. Indeed, at many of the meetings I have attended parts of this resolution were the subject matter of keen and intelligent discussion. I certainly think the minister and the government are to be complimented on the introduction of the resolution.
Something has been said about the principle of the benefit of the doubt. It would seem to me that this is a term which has a definite and specific connotation in the minds of the courts and lawyers. In any case where there is a dispute between the crown and a subject or citizen, when all the evidence has been introduced and is before a tribunal, if it is difficult for the tribunal to formulate a firm decision then the benefit of the doubt must be given to the citizen as against the crown. That is something which has come down to us through generations and centuries of our legal experience in common law. I would think that the intention of those who drafted this particular section must have been guided to this particular phrase and its meaning. I certainly hope that from and after the introduction of this resolution that principle will be applied.
I want to deal briefly with something which I think should be mentioned at this time. It was raised by members from Newfoundland. Let me say first, as a condition precedent, that I had the privilege of serving both in this country and overseas with Newfoundlanders who were in the Canadian forces. They were the best of soldiers and the best of people. Certainly there is no reason, as the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo has said, why they should not be entitled to be put in precisely the same position as other Canadians.
However, there is a right way and a wrong way in which to achieve that end. When we come to consider the invitations which were 90205-6-1194
Pension Act
extended by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate and others, I suggest that they are in fact inviting this government to violate the sanctity of the British North America Act. I had the privilege of hearing the speech of the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I also read what he had to say, and I did so carefully. He referred to section 38 or, as he called it, term 38 which, as he said correctly, is part of a schedule attached to the British North America Act amendment of 1949. As such it becomes part of our constitution and cannot be in any way amended or changed save by the method laid out and provided by practice and by the British North America Act itself. That is particularly so where this is in fact a contract between two parties.
The hon. member made that suggestion because there was not contained within the four corners of term 38 the provision that he considered should be there, namely that veterans who prior to 1949 had not applied for and obtained a pension should not be compelled to go to the United Kingdom, obtain the pension which would be payable pursuant to the regulations of that country, and then come back to Canada to have it supplemented to the same level as that of Canadian veterans. I think he has a case there. There is a point there, but that is not the question.
I have read term 38 quite carefully, and twist, contort and torture it as you will, you cannot at any time read that interpretation into it. I think it would be quite wrong for this or any government to be asked to place an incorrect interpretation, no matter with what laudable motive, on a portion of the constitution with the intention that it should achieve a desirable result.
The other alternative suggested was this. If you cannot interpret it in that way, why not introduce in these amendments to the Pension Act a section or a provision which would give this particular privilege, or would restore to these veterans the same privileges that apply to other Canadians? I take it that would be nothing but a unilateral declaration by the Canadian government as to part of the constitution. As I say, the motive may be quite laudable, but I am quite certain that no province, and particularly the province of Newfoundland, would welcome an attempt by this government to so deal with this particular matter.
It seems to me that if we are to achieve this result it may be necessary to seek a proper constitutional amendment. I suppose for the next 20 years this government may be compelled to pick up the bits and pieces of the legislation of the previous government and remedy its defects. I think we may as well start now, by doing it in a proper

Pension Act
way when we have to do it. For that reason I support what was said by the hon. member for Saskatoon, that this is a serious matter which should engage the attention of the Department of Justice. When we attempt to achieve for the people of Newfoundland those things to which they are entitled, it should be done in the proper way.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in this debate I have no intention of delaying unduly the passage of this resolution, but in view of the contribution made in both the first and second world wars by men and women from my constituency I feel I have a definite obligation to speak at this time.
I should like first of all to associate myself with what was said by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs when he spoke in this house on December 12, congratulating his predecessor, now a member of the other place, on the work he had done in connection with veterans legislation. Colonel Brooks, now Senator Brooks, was a distinguished member of the armed services in two world wars and a distinguished member of the opposition before he became minister of veterans affairs. I can assure this committee that at all times Colonel Brooks held the interest of the veterans as his first consideration.
It has been my privilege to serve as a member of the standing committee on veterans affairs for the past three sessions and again this session. We Canadians, and this parliament of Canada, owe a great deal to those men and women who, without considering the sacrifice, gave of their best in the cause of freedom. We do not discharge our obligations to them by erecting cenotaphs, monuments or placing marble plaques
Pension Act
in our public buildings. These might bear mute though eloquent testimony to the memory of those they commemorate, but they do not compensate for the sacrifices which those people made incidental to the conflict in which they were engaged. I realize that we cannot measure suffering, hardship and sacrifice in terms of money. However, we can, as far as we are able, provide that those who suffered shall not be in a worse position than those who did not make sacrifices.
Many of our veterans-and a great deal of credit is due to them-came back from the conflict and were able to rehabilitate themselves satisfactorily. Others were not, and it is to them that we must be always ready and willing to lend a sympathetic ear and a helping hand. Since 1957 this government has been most arduous in its legislation and activities concerning pension benefits. I do not intend to review in any detail what has been done. Previous speakers have indicated some of the work which has been carried out by this government since 1957. We had a forecast by the Prime Minister some time ago that there would be an increase in pension benefits, and the resolution before us provides for such increases, provides for better appeal provisions and provides also for other fringe benefits.
This is not a problem which is lessening. The problem of veterans and their treatment is one which is growing and will continue to grow as the veterans become older. The former minister of veterans affairs, speaking to the Canadian Legion at its annual convention, said, as reported at page 12 of the pamphlet containing his speech:
In 1920 there were about 570.000 veterans of what was then known as the great war. By 1945 this number was down to around 350,000 but world war II had added a million new ones.
Later in the course of the same speech the former minister said:
In 1950 it was estimated that there were around 200,000 world war I veterans under age 60, and about 110,000 over that age. There were then about 35.000 war veterans allowances in payment, for which the annual liability was just over $24 millions.
Dealing with the present position he said:
Let us look ahead now over the next 15 years, by which time we estimate that about 80.000 great war veterans will be living in Canada, and that around 200,000 world war II veterans will be over age 60.
Then to quote further:
To peer further into the future is difficult, but we can predict fairly accurately, from mortality tables, the veteran population of Canada for any particular year. For example, we estimate that, in 1980, there will be 342,000 world war II veterans aged 60 and over; and that the largest number of veterans in that age group-515,000-will occur in 1986.

Pension Act
Hon. members will see from these figures that this is a growing problem and one which must be met from day to day. I would suggest, as others have suggested to the minister, that a similar resolution dealing with war allowance provisions be introduced in order that an increase in pensions may not mean, in effect, a decrease in war allowance payments. I would also suggest that the war allowance ceiling be raised so that those veterans who are desirous of earning more might be in a position to do so.
A great deal has been said about the benefit of the doubt clause. As hon. members have pointed out, this is quite a familiar phrase to those of us who are lawyers, but no judge has been able to define precisely or satisfactorily "what is a reasonable doubt." We interpret it as meaning that if after all the evidence has been heard there is any doubt on the whole case, or on any phase of it, that doubt must be resolved in favour of the accused person. I think the same interpretation should apply to applications for a pension before the pension commission. If there is any doubt on any phase of the medical evidence, and that is the prime factor, it should be given in favour of the applicant.
I should also like to suggest that the procedure on appeal be made simpler; that provision be made for the introduction of new evidence, if necessary, before the appeal board. I do hope that when the bill is considered in committee these and other matters will be dealt with. I want to assure the veterans of my constituency and veterans generally that any reasonable request by them will be given every consideration.

Mr. Chairman, it is appropriate that I should say a few words on this occasion. My province had the highest percentage of volunteers of any area of Canada and my riding, of course, was very well represented in that regard. We have a very large number of legionnaires throughout the riding, and the Summerside Legion branch has one of the finest Legion homes and is one of the best branches in Canada.
I should also like to extend my congratulations to the new Minister of Veterans Affairs and his parliamentary secretary. The former minister, Colonel Alfred Brooks, was well known in my province, and I am sure that many veterans, as well as the members of this house, will wish him success in his new post.
A great deal has been said about the increased benefits that have been granted to veterans in the last few years, and I do not intend to review this other than to comment that they have been a source of great satisfaction to myself. This new legislation will add further benefits to those already granted.

However, there are several remarks that I should like to make, and in particular I should like to refer to the veteran who receives a disability pension and the remainder of whose income is made up of a war veterans allowance. It is imperative that the War Veterans' Allowance Act be reviewed at an early date to permit deserving veterans to obtain the benefit of the legislation now before the house. I am sure that the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the government will listen to members from all sides of the house who have made this recommendation.
The remainder of the resolution deals with the benefit of the doubt and administration. I think possibly, sir, I can illustrate my feelings in this regard by referring to a number of cases about which I have been in contact with the Canadian pension commission. Here perhaps I can point out to my constituents that the pension commission is an independent organization and removed from the Minister of Veterans Affairs. The commission makes its own decisions and not the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
One case that I find most particularly annoying concerns a young chap who volunteered early in the war and proceeded overseas as a dispatch rider. He was injured in a motorcycle accident one evening; he was taken to an English civilian hospital, spent some time in hospital, returned to his unit and was on light duty. After his discharge he began to suffer pains in the back of his head where he had been injured in the accident. He got in touch with the Canadian pension commission for a pension. They took the attitude that the pains in the back of his head were imaginary, and he has been going back and forth for renewal hearings for the last 12 years. With the assistance of Colonel Brooks I was able to get him admitted to Camp Hill Hospital for an examination by specialists at that institution. He was examined by a neurologist, who reported that there was definitely trauma and that it was the source of the pain. However, six weeks later he received a phone call from another member of the medical staff who pointed out that in an interview with him the veteran had stated that he was in hospital a month and that was incorrect, and for no apparent reason the neurologist reversed his decision and the veteran is still attempting to get his pension.
Last year I wrote to the Canadian pension commission about this case. I referred them to the benefit of the doubt section and also to the earlier report of the neurologist, together with the fact that it has been impossible to obtain records from the English civilian hospital. After the renewal hearing they made the same decision. On checking his records, sir, at the renewal hearing I find that one

member of the commission has sat on each of his several renewal hearings. I think that points up a number of things that have been mentioned by members in this debate, namely the apparent disregard for the benefit of the doubt, the need of a new system of appeal, and the numerous cases in which medical documentation is not complete.
Another case that I would like to refer to concerns another young chap who served in Italy in 1944. He began to complain of chest pains and shortness of breath. He was examined by a medical officer. In all fairness to the medical officer it must be pointed out that the examination was probably conducted under anything but satisfactory conditions. The doctor attributed the chest pains and shortness of breath to a nervous condition. The young man returned to Canada after the war and shortly after discharge he suffered a heart attack. He was forced to sell his business and his wife was compelled to go to work to earn a living for him. In this case the Canadian pension commission ruled that the cardiac condition was pre-enlistment and was not aggravated during service.
I am sure that a great many veterans who made the tour through Italy would disagree with that decision. In addition, the pension commission has completely ignored his complaints of 1944, which I think point to aggravation of a heart condition whether or not it was pre-enlistment.
Recently I had the opportunity of talking with a former medical officer of the Royal Canadian Navy. He was relating some of his experiences, and referred to the fact that he often wonders about the present documentation. He told me the story of a convoy arriving in Newfoundland after a very difficult crossing of the Atlantic, and in a short while he was expected to examine 140 men. He often wonders now about the documentation. He states that it was impossible for him to make an adequate examination and at the same time enter his findings on the individual's documents.
Therefore I submit that the pension commission must bear these matters in mind and not depend entirely upon the medical documentation. I am hopeful that when the legislation is presented to the house it will provide the means to correct these injustices, and I look forward to seeing the legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take much time. I was a soldier in the first world war. I did not win the war, although I was there. I am pleased with the appointment of the new Minister of Veterans Affairs, because he is a man who fought in two wars and he knows what it is all about.
I am not going to take much time because I should like to see the bill passed. All I want
Pension Act
is to see the allowance large enough so that the recipient will get a decent living. When we went overseas it was said that "nothing is too good for you" and afterwards the veterans said, "Wasn't it true? Nothing was too good."

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak briefly on the resolution I want to echo the congratulations extended by previous speakers to the new minister, his predecessor, the minister's parliamentary secretary and the other illustrious ministers who have been charged with the administration of this department in past years. I think it has generally been the case that capable men with the experience necessary to take charge of this department have always been found.
I wish to make a couple of observations. I am not a veteran. I was precluded from serving because of a serious illness, and I have always felt as I move amongst veterans today and meet them on the occasion of various celebrations that they have something of which I am very jealous. They have earned it and I did not, and I am pleased to have the opportunity from time to time to mingle with them, to listen to their experiences and their problems and to be as helpful as I can in bringing about justice for some of them where injustice seems to prevail.
From that point of view I think I can make an observation which I am sure will be fully supported. I believe that the grateful people of Canada desire that, through legislation passed by parliament, their gratitude and their regard for the veterans be shown in an adequate and substantial manner. I believe that has generally been the intent of parliament in the legislation that has been passed and revised from time to time in order to keep it up to date so as to meet the problems of the veterans.

Pension Act
We all must realize that as time goes on and veterans become older, their problems are greater. Some of them who have had companions to help them through life have lost them, and their present position in the twilight years becomes almost untenable without sincerity, sympathy and help being extended to them.
I raise my voice at this time because I believe parliament always intended that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the veteran. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that members are not wasting the time of the committee by speaking in numbers on this occasion. We are making the desire and intention of parliament known to those charged with the administration of the act. I cannot believe that these people have heard the voice of parliament in this regard and fully understand our desire. When some 50 per cent to 52 per cent of appeals from their decisions are allowed, it indicates to me a great lack of judgment in the initial consideration of these cases.
This is a serious matter to the veteran concerned. I have run across some of these cases which have been delayed for weeks and weeks and even months and months because of appeals and the fact that new evidence has been demanded. This is all right if the veteran is in a fair state of competence, but in many of these cases he has reached the point in the road which brought about the application in the first place, and the longer attention to and decision on the application is delayed the more serious the problem of the veteran becomes. In making these observations I do so in the hope that the addition of my voice to those of hon. members who have already spoken will bring about a more positive interpretation of the will of parliament by the administrators of the act.
I am very proud of the veterans organizations that exist in my community; I think they are among the finest in the country. The number of members of the house who are veterans indicates to me that, having served in war, they are not neglecting their responsibilities in times of peace and are discharging those responsibilities most efficiently.
The Canadian Legion, in particular the Saskatchewan command and our own Regina branch, has done an admirable job in so far as I am aware through my own work. They have gone to all lengths to properly attend to the demands made upon them by the veterans and their dependents. I do not know of a case in which they have let the veteran down. The results of their representations have not always been those for which we hoped, but at least I can say to all veterans and their dependents in Regina and in the

province that they have been given the most adequate service through their Legion branches.
I should like to make one other observation, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the allowances. I do not believe it would be fair, reasonable or satisfactory if this part of the legislation were to be improved at this session and the war veterans allowances forgotten. I seriously urge upon the minister the bringing up to date of the war veterans allowances at this session.

I feel that the debate on this resolution could not possibly be complete without a few words from me on behalf of the veterans in the Vegreville constituency. There are a great many branches of the Legion there, and all are well attended. I can assure you that there is strong support amongst the veterans of this area for the present Department of Veterans Affairs.
Before I go any further I should like to congratulate our new minister upon his appointment to this department, the department about which there is the least controversy. It really is wonderful to find that when veterans affairs are being discussed everybody, whatever their political affiliations, wholeheartedly supports legislation for the benefit of the veterans. It is too bad that other departments could not receive the same treatment. At the same time I should like to convey my personal congratulations to the former minister, Colonel Brooks, on his elevation to his new post. He did a wonderful job when he was minister. He was always a great advocate for the rights of the ex-servicemen, and I am sure that everyone here wishes him well in his new post.
There is actually very little more to be said about this resolution, Mr. Chairman. Almost everything that could be said has been said and my remarks, therefore, will be very brief. When the minister brought this resolution before us on December 12 I was extremely pleased with its wording. I refer especially to the part which reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Pension Act to provide for increases to disabled veterans and their dependents; to permit payment of supplementary pensions in certain cases; to permit appeals from decisions of the former board of pension commissioners; and to provide for certain further changes in connection with the administration of the act.
Those things are all good, and they are the things the veterans have been wanting. At the same time it must not be forgotten that in 1957 the war pensioners of Canada received an increase in pensions which amounted to some $47.5 million. These increases were granted to approximately 150,000 pensioners of the two world wars and

Korea. It is gratifying to know that pension increases are being granted to the veterans, and I trust that these increases will be adequate to look after their requirements. The widows' allowances, allowances to dependent parents, allowances for educational purposes and so on, are also to be increased. I believe this provision will be of great help to these people who carried on their shoulders the weight of the actual fighting in the war. There will be increases also in the amounts paid for hospitalization.
I should like to conclude by saying that a good many veterans will be very happy when the War Veterans Allowance Act is reviewed and those people who have served their country well will become eligible for larger payments. All veterans of Canada will be interested to know that since the Conservative government came into power in 1957 many things

have been done to help them. The Pension Act was thoroughly reviewed. The last previous increase in pensions had been effective January 1, 1952 and a revision was desirable. They actually worked when they probably should not have been working. However, they wanted to be on their own. They were extremely independent. However, age has more or less slipped up on them and they are quite old now. I certainly think that any benefit of the doubt should be resolved in their favour. At the risk of incurring the displeasure and perhaps causing the discomfiture of hon. members whose interest in this resolution seems to be of a passing nature, may I say there are two items upon which I should like to comment. It is true that a number of the members of this House of Commons have spoken but in my opinion there are two things which should be underlined. First of all, there is in the Pension 
Act a provision which is of a mildly permissive nature whereby the department or the minister may provide domiciliary care for veterans who, for a number of reasons, are unable to look after themselves either because of age or illness. They are not men who are ill in the true sense of the word, in that they should occupy active treatment beds in veterans hospitals. In Edmonton we have one such home for veterans at the former government house.
I must draw to the attention of the members of this committee the fact that this is a well run and happy establishment. Unfortunately, however, it is only about a third of the size required, with the result that active treatment beds in our veterans hospitals in the region are occupied by men who would be far happier and far better looked after in such a type of establishment. I am sure that there are many other regions within the country where this could be done.
As a result of world war I we are now getting a greater number of men in this age category and in this particular category of chronic illness. They are the responsibility of society in one way or another. There is no way of trying to sweep their condition under any carpet. They are veterans. They served their country. Many of them are suffering from advanced age or increased disability because of the rigours of their war service many years ago. If we do not look after them in domiciliary care establishments, they must go on relief or they must be placed in some other public institution; but wherever they are they are still the responsibility of society. I would put it to the members of this committee that their true place is under the wing of the Department of Veterans Affairs. I would suggest to the minister that this is one area of fruitful inquiry in order to see whether the department could not extend its facilities for this particular group of veterans.
Before long there will also be an increasing number of veterans of world war II who may fit into this category. It is not merely a matter of a transitory stage where you can deal with a group of men over a short period of time.
The second point I wish to make is one that has been adverted to by a number of hon. members who have spoken this afternoon, I refer to the benefit of the doubt provision under the Pensions Act. Since my entering parliament in 1957 I believe 90 per cent of the cases of trouble with veterans pensions that have been referred to me have dealt with this difficult position of veterans of world war I where medical examinations on discharge were of a cursory nature, where records were scanty or practically nonexistent and where the initial work of the

pension commission was rather restrictive. We all know-and we need not hide this knowledge-that the initial handling of veterans pensions was rather difficult. Fortunately there has been a change of philosophy and a change of mentality so that veterans now get a better break. The condition is not quite the same with veterans of world war II. Their documentation is in much better shape and they receive much better medical examinations.
For instance, upon coming out of prisoner of war camp I underwent four days of extensive medical examination, and within three months I went through another three days of examination prior to discharge. So there is plenty on record in so far as I am concerned. I am sure that is the experience of most men who came out of the forces after world war II. It is to the credit of the Department of National Defence, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the authorities that this was done. I am sure it is going to save a great deal of trouble in the future.
I wish to come back to the position of these elderly veterans of world war I, and particularly this matter of the 50 per cent disability and whether the widow is entitled to a continuing pension. If her husband did not receive a 50 per cent disability pension, or unless he dies of wounds directly attributable to his war service she is not entitled to any pension. This has caused a great deal of hardship and I am sure there are many, many cases where a little more humane, a little more intelligent interpretation of the facts and a little more generous interpretation of the benefit of the doubt clause would relieve a great deal of this hardship. After all, the alternative for a great many of these people is to become a charge on the state somewhere along the line. Why not bring them under their proper category here under veterans affairs? The cost all comes out of the same pocket eventually, that of the taxpayer.
There is only one thing further I wish to say in this connection. In many cases when the decision of the pension commission is anounced that the disability is not attributable to war service, or that the condition is not aggravated by war service, there has been a long lapse of time. I would put it to the members of this house that in world war II particularly there were large numbers of prisoners of war. I know from personal experience that many of my fellow prisoners of war are now developing symptoms of maladies which are attributable to the time they spent as prisoners of war. They were told by doctors that this might happen. I remember in my own case I was told I was perfectly 90205-6-120J
Pension Act
all right, but that perhaps 15 or 20 years hence something might develop.
I would underline this particular point. That in the case of former prisoners of war or men who have undergone rather rigorous experiences where the after-effects may be delayed, a good, hard look should be given to their present circumstances, and their conditions should be interpreted in the light of those circumstances.
As a member of the Montgomery branch No. 24 of the Canadian Legion, which lays claim to the largest membership of any Canadian Legion branch in Canada, it is my great pleasure to address the members of this house this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I am rising simply because of a statement made by the hon. member for Nanaimo, who I am sure had no intention of misrepresenting the record when he said there had been no change since 1952 in the scale of pensions until this government came into power. In brief, the basic monthly scale for total disability under the Pension Act will be increased from $125 to $150, or if married from $170 to $200. I, too, would like to say a few words at this time on behalf of the veterans of Canada. In the riding I have the honour to represent there are 16 branches of the Canadian Legion. It has been my privilege on many occasions to visit meetings of these branches and attend their social gatherings, and may I say right now that there is no finer group of Canadians today than the members of the Canadian Legion. I have had heart to heart talks with many of these men and I know that if another war were to start tomorrow these same men would be willing to defend their country and loved ones again.
I cannot stress too strongly the importance of this measure. As has been stated already in this committee, I am sure that all the Canadian people will be proud to share their portion of the cost of this legislation.
May I now turn to another urgent question and one which I think merits immediate consideration, namely the need to give re-boards to many of our Canadian veterans? I know many veterans who are definitely entitled to a pension but who, because of previous decisions and red tape which is apparently insurmountable, have been unable to qualify. As a result, they have been deprived of justice. I am certain that consideration of this question is uppermost in the mind of the Minister of Veterans Affairs, a man who can and will speak from authority becauses of his own personal experience.

I4r. Churchill: There has been general acceptance of this resolution. The committee has expressed itself in favour of increases being made in pensions for disabled veterans and of certain other alterations being made to the act. Details in this respect will be before
Pension Act
us shortly, I hope. The debate, as it has proceeded, and the many cases which have been cited, have shown that the problem of veterans is a continuing one.
We still have a few survivors of the South African war. There are the veterans of the first world war, the veterans of the second world war and the veterans of the Korean war. Then, of course, there are those who have served or are serving in various posts throughout the world either under NATO or for the United Nations and who, though not necessarily engaged in conflict, are running certain risks with regard to health. Then, again, we must not forget those who suffer injury or disablement in the course of their regular duties in the armed forces. These eventually end up within the scope of this particular act in some instances because of the dangerous nature of the occupations in which they are engaged. Thus we have a continuing problem which must be faced and met by parliament, and which has been met by parliament over the years.
At the same time we have to recognize that the problems which continually arise are not easily solved. Example after example has been given to us in the course of the last two days of difficult, marginal cases where in the opinion of the hon. member speaking something further should have been done. So although the Pension Act has been in existence for a long time and although about 40 years of experience has been acquired with regard to dealing with veterans, in the year 1961 we are nevertheless still made aware of the problems of veterans.
We have not reached final solution with regard to some of these matters. I think it is commendable that so many members have taken an interest in this piece of legislation. It is commendable that the Canadian Legion and other veterans organizations have presented briefs to whichever government was in power, year after year, bringing to the attention of the government the problems of veterans and suggestions as to solving those problems.
The veterans' contribution, either through members here in the House of Commons, or through organizations across the country, has been of substantial assistance to our comrades in arms who suffered more than most of us during the course of their service overseas. We have a continuing obligation to them, which we can fulfil in part through our activity here in the House of Commons and through amending legislation where that appears to be necessary.
Time will not permit me, Mr. Chairman, to deal with some of the particular problems which were raised by many who spoke. The

Pension Act
problem raised by the members from Newfoundland, although it perhaps should have been decided long before this, is something that is rather new to me; it has come to my attention within the last few months and I have been looking into it. The standing committee on veterans affairs should look at this problem again this session.
The same thing applies to war veterans allowances. Although many members mentioned that that act is not under consideration at this moment, there is a danger of confusing people's minds in a discussion of the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Pension Act. Nevertheless, again the standing committee on veterans affairs can consider it and make suggestions. I will go this far and say that already commencing in November, I have instituted a study of the War Veterans Allowance Act to see what is required in the way of amendments thereto and to consider how quickly those amendments might be undertaken. I can make no promises; I am making no promises at this time. I am indicating that I have the matter under advisement and have instituted the necessary study, and I am making a study myself of the War Veterans Allowance Act.
With regard to other problems of veterans that were mentioned, such as merchant seamen, gallantry awards, South African veterans and so on, those are problems which we cannot discuss adequately when we are dealing with amendments to the Pension Act, but the standing committee on veterans affairs can look at these matters and bring them to the attention of myself and of the house. There will be another opportunity, of course, and that is when the estimates of the Depart-met of Veterans Affairs are before the committee.
There is one subject that was touched upon by most of the members who spoke in the course of the debate, and that is the application of the benefit of the doubt clause in the Pension Act. They did this, as I understand it, not in criticism of the pension commission, which is held in high regard by members of parliament. Over the years the pension commission and its predecessor, the board of pension commissioners, performed a very valuable service and an extremely arduous one in assessing the cases that came before them. I do not think anyone is critical in a serious way of the pension commission.
On the other hand, the members, as I assess what they have been saying during the last two days, think that the pension commission perhaps has not interpreted the benefit of the doubt clause in the way in which people have expected it to be interpreted. I think it has been said on many occasions that the benefit of

the doubt clause has entered into the consideration of the pension commissioners whenever they have had a case before them; but this is an old and continuing problem, and I hope that we can look at it again this year in the standing committee on veterans affairs and in consultation with the pension commission.
As hon. members have rightly pointed out, the commission is an independent body, and properly so. It derives its authority from parliament. It is not subject to the influence of the minister or of any member and makes its own decision and its own interpretation of the act which grants it authority. That being so, our job here as members of the House of Commons is to give assistance to the pension commission, either by amendment of the act under which they operate or by indicating to them the purpose and intent of parliament, as we understand it, with regard to their interpretation of the act. They may not accept our advice, but, on the other hand, I think it would not hurt for them to be aware of the understanding that members of parliament have with regard to this particular clause, clause 70, of the Pension Act. The clause has a long history. I have looked into that history. In 1930 a special committee sat on the problems of pensions and returned soldiers' problems and reported in 1930. The chairman of that committee was the Hon. C. G. Power. It was as a result of that committee's investigation that the benefit of the doubt clause was incorporated in the statutes. When the committee submitted its report, and I am quoting now from page 420 of the report of the special committee on pensions and returned soldiers' problems, it stated as follows:
In addition to the foregoing questions of organization and procedure the committee proposes the enactment of a general rule governing the commission, the pension tribunal and the appeal court, whereby all reasonable inferences are to be drawn in favour of the applicant, who is to be given the benefit of the doubt, the rules stating that the applicant is to be relieved from the obligation of giving conclusive evidence in favour of his right, an obligation which it is in many cases quite impossible for him to discharge.
Before reaching this conclusion the committee heard from many eminent witnesses. Some of the examples that we have heard in the house today are similar to the examples given 31 years ago by people who appeared before that committee. General Sir Arthur Currie, who was then living, gave an example of a signaller, and I quote:
He was 37 years of age, big, strong and in perfect physical condition.
That is when he enlisted. General Currie then went on to describe the conditions under which he served in France, as follows:
Day and night, rain or shine, he must get out and keep the lines repaired. It is not a case of eight

or 10 hours a day, it is a case of 24 hours a day, and for days on end, always working in the battle area. His shelter at the best of times is nothing more than a thin sheet of corrugated iron or an old piece of tarpaulin; it may be nothing more than a shell hole in the broken and poisoned earth. Yet that man must be out all the time in all kinds of weather, wet to the skin, cold, lousy. If he does occupy a rude dug-out the chances are he has rats for companions. He is always in the battle area, shelled and bombed. Do you mean to tell me that those conditions will not affect adversely a man's health?
Then he went on to give the subsequent history of this chap who suffered certain pains and extreme nervousness and was considered to have sciatica for which he received a pension. Subsequently his case was looked at again and was diagnosed as spinal arthritis for which no permanent cure could be effected. In those bad days the board had to reach the conclusion that they could not recognize spinal arthritis as a pensionable disability, so the man lost his pension for sciatica and received nothing at all. The benefit of the doubt clause was incorporated into the act in order to remove that type of difficulty.
The second case, and the only other one I will give, was recalled to my mind by the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West who mentioned prisoners of war. There was an instance given in 1930 of a man who had enlisted at the age of 35. In front of Regina trench down on the Somme he received three machine gun bullets in the right leg, fracturing the tibia, and he also received one in the right shoulder. He lay in a shell hole under terrible conditions for four days. The only thing he had to drink was poisoned water in the shell hole. There were two other men in the shell hole with him and one died and the other went mad. This man was hit on Sunday and taken prisoner on the following Thursday. He was treated in Germany, had six operations, was repatriated through Switzerland and had one operation there and one in England. He was returned as a stretcher case to Canada and discharged in 1919 with a 15 per cent pension for the wound in his leg. During his time as a prisoner he developed a stomach condition. No record is available of his medical history while he was a prisoner of war. It is not available to anyone. He developed a stroke. It was decided by the federal appeal board that it was hemiplegia from which he suffered and they gave their orders as follows:
After consideration of the evidence and record the board finds that cerebral hemorrhage resulting in hemiplegia is not attributed to military service. The appeal is disallowed.
These are two examples from that year. Members today have given other examples from the present time. The benefit of the doubt clause was incorporated into the act
Pension Act
to make provision for men who could not provide documentary evidence as to the hazards they underwent when they were overseas, whether in the first war or the second, and many men in the second world war suffered just as grievously as men in the first war and suffered from exposure in just the same way. In 1930 that clause was introduced into the act and subsequently it has been amended on three occasions. It will not take me very long to put on the record the four versions of the benefit of the doubt clause so that anyone looking at this debate in the future will have a ready reference. In the 1930 statutes of Canada the section read as follows:
73. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
In 1946 an amendment was made, the section was renumbered 63 and it read as follows:
63. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
The change there was the addition of the words "and presumptions". In 1948 a further change was made, and section 63 of the 1948 statutes read as follows:
63. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
The change there was from "shall be entitled to draw" to "shall draw". Finally in 1952 another change was made. The section now is numbered 70 and it reads as follows:
70. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant is entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which means that it is not necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
The change there is the introduction of the words "is entitled to" instead of "shall be entitled to". I put these four versions on

Pension Act
the record for the benefit of those who are interested in this problem to show the effort that has been made from 1930 to 1952 to amend the benefit of the doubt clause so that it will be more suitable in the circumstances in which the board of pension commissioners has to apply it. My judgment is that no matter how frequently we amend the clause the question will still be determined on the basis of interpretation, and that is precisely what General Currie said in 1930. That is how it is applied.
All that I can say further in regard to this matter is that from the number of members who have spoken about the benefit of the doubt clause and from the interest that has been shown in the application of that clause the pension commissioners may reasonably reach the conclusion that parliament is seriously interested in-what shall I say-a generous application of the benefit of the doubt clause. In the ten years that I have been here I have heard no complaint about the pension commission being overgenerous in granting money from the treasury to applicants for pension, and I think they have been very sound in that regard. We are not asking them to lower the barriers and let anybody in. Bona fide cases, as they have considered them in the past, should be the ones on which the board will finally adjudicate, but in these bona fide cases where men have actually served and have suffered from their service I think it is the opinion of parliament that the benefit of the doubt clause should apply.
As some members have said, it certainly should apply in the case of the older world war I veterans. Many of these men, because of an independence of character that cynical people do not sometimes recognize, have refused over the years to accept a pension or to report for pension purposes and now that they are in their 70's they are beginning to find that it might have been wiser to report for examination in days gone by.
A very close friend of mine who has since died comes to my mind. He was a 30 per cent pensioner and should have been an 80 per cent pensioner all his life but he never gave up during the course of his experience from 1917 until just two or three years ago. He was granted an 80 per cent pension when he finally appeared at an advanced age before a board of examiners. He was typical of many men who served overseas in the first world war, men who simply would not admit that they needed assistance from anyone. These older veterans of the first world war cannot produce documents. There were no filing cabinets available on the field of action during the first world war, and I think it is the feeling of the committee that

those men who cannot produce evidence should have the benefit of the doubt. I say this, bearing in mind these two cases which were brought before the commission in 1930.
I argued this matter in the House of Commons in 1953, 1954 and before the estimates committee in 1955. I have argued at different times that the benefit of the doubt should be applied to first world war veterans who suffered from the effects of gas. Many men who suffered gas attacks in the first world war ended up in the hospital. Others got as far as the dressing station and were returned to their units, while still others did not report at all. Who is to say that years later the effects of this poison gas do not seriously destroy their physical functions? Medical opinion may say that there are no after effects of poison gas. Unless medical opinion will quite flatly state that, then I used to argue, and I would be inclined to argue now, that the pension commission should give the benefit of the doubt to a man who could show, through the action in which his regiment was engaged or through affidavits from his companions that he was subjected to the effects of poison gas.
This is just another example that relates to veterans of the first world war. As time goes on I think there will be less trouble with second world war veterans because the records have been much more adequately kept. The hon. member for Greenwood will recall that when he returned in 1918 or 1919, I suppose, like the rest of us, all he had to say was that he was A-l and he could get on board ship. If he did not say he was A-l he had to stay in England or France until further notice. This was the easy way, I think, of getting discharged in 1919. In 1946 it was not nearly as easy. You had to go through a very stiff medical board before you were released, so I think we will have less trouble in the future with the veterans of the second world war than we have had with those in the earlier conflict whose records were not complete.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman I would just say that the veterans of Canada should be pleased at the interest the committee has taken in this problem during the last two days. I believe the veterans of Canada are well represented here on both sides of the house. There has been a serious interest in this measure, and we have not engaged in more than just a mild flurry of political interchange. I would have loved to have taken part in one exchange that occurred a while ago, but I thought I would abstain and save it for some other occasion because we are not in a controversial field when we are dealing with veterans problems. I feel that all of us here, no matter what party

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
we represent, have an interest m veterans. We recognize what they have done and the service that they have given to their country.
I feel it was a privilege to serve. This is not said very often by veterans, but now I am getting to an age where I think perhaps I can say some of these things. It is a privilege to serve. Many men who would have liked to have served were denied that privilege. I think veterans should recognize that fact and consider it a real privilege to have been physically fit and able to serve their country in time of distress. Nobody would think now of glorifying war or anything of that nature. We hope that our efforts during this twentieth century will result in permanent peace. At the same time we have to stand ready to cope with whatever perils may confront us in the future.
These men whom we have been considering during the last few days, the disability pensioners, the men who actually suffered, are the ones who have set the example for young Canada to follow. May we not forget them or their dependents during the course of their lives. They gave in the service of their country, and it is up to the country to play its part now. The Pension Act which we are amending will in part, and only in part, repay to our disability pensioners the debt that Canada owes them.
