speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is only eight months since the debate took place on my department's estimates for the fiscal year 1960-61. At that time I reviewed and explained in some detail the attitude and general policy of this government, so far as immigration is concerned. The report on my remarks at that time will be found commencing on page 4711 of Hansard for June 9, 1960. The outline of policy which I presented at that time is still valid and I do not think that I need to take the time of the committee by repeating now what I said on that occasion. I shall therefore limit my remarks to a few brief comments on the most
1900	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration significant developments in the immigration field during the period which has elapsed since we last discussed these estimates.
The final reports for 1960 show that the total of immigrants admitted to Canada during the calendar year was 104,111- This figure shows very little change from the previous year, 1959, when 106,928 immigrants came forward. During the discussion of estimates in June last I indicated that it was then my expectation that the numbers coming forward in 1960 would be slightly in excess of those for the previous year. On a month to month basis the actual number of immigrants coming forward during 1960 was slightly ahead of 1959 up to the end of September. From that point on the figures took a downward turn, owing in part to the prevalence of buoyant economic and employment conditions in the European countries from which we draw most of our immigrants; and also in part to the fact that many of the sponsors in Canada, faced with uncertainty as to their own employment situation in Canada during the winter months, were less inclined to press forward with their applications to bring forward their relatives from overseas. This situation is normal and understandable in view of the difficulty economic circumstances through which we are now passing in this country, contrasted with the usual economic and employment opportunities reported from so many of the countries of Europe.
Despite the over-all slight decrease in the total movement of immigrants to Canada, we experienced in 1960 in certain sectors small gains, which are gratifying and give encouragement for the future. There was a slight upturn during 1960 in the movements from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Germany. Traditionally we look to the United Kingdom to supply a larger number of immigrants annually than we usually receive from any other country; and during 1960 the position of the United Kingdom was very largely, though not completely, restored to its accustomed position in first place among the countries of origin of our immigrant population. Actually the final totals for the year show that 20,853 British immigrants came to Canada in 1960 which was an increase of approximately 1,500 over 1959, whereas 21,308 Italian immigrants were admitted-they were the second group-with the Italian movement slipping past the British total by a small margin during the final month of 1960.
The most noteworthy decreases were in the movement of Italian and Chinese immigrants, the last mentioned decline being undoubtedly the result of a sharp falling off in the number of applications for admission, which in turn was probably a consequence of the investigation into illegal Chinese immigration, which


was actively under way during most of 1960. Other small but encouraging increases took place in the movements from Austria, Finland, France, Portugal and Yugoslavia. With one or two exceptions, there is probably nothing particularly significant about these individual fluctuations, except to show that there is a continuing interest in the possibilities of continued emigration to Canada among the nationals of many countries, and that we continue to be in a position where we can encourage and stimulate suitable increases in these movements when economic and other circumstances justify.
I am sure that there will be general agreement with the proposition that Canada should continue to maintain its position over the years as a country which welcomes considerable numbers of suitable immigrants to its shores and I am personally satisfied that, even in the face of formidable economic difficulties, we have succeeded in maintaining our position in this regard during 1960.
I think it is important for us to keep in mind in this connection that, by maintaining a suitable flow of immigrants to Canada, we not only provide better economic opportunities for these immigrants themselves, but we also add to the economic productivity, the employment opportunities and the national wealth of Canada as a whole.
A great deal of emphasis has been placed in recent months on the question of employment and unemployment, and concern has been expressed that we should not develop a situation in Canada which through large scale immigration increases the difficulties of providing employment for those already in Canada. This is a legitimate concern but there are other aspects to this question which need to be taken into account if the situation is to be viewed in the proper perspective.
It is, for example, significant to note that of the 104,000 persons who came to Canada as immigrants in 1960 almost half were persons, chiefly wives and other dependants, who were not destined to the labour force. Over 8,000 of the 53,000 immigrants destined to the labour force were in the managerial and professional categories. Large numbers of the others were in the clerical, commercial, service and agricultural fields, with a sharp decline in the labourer classification, most of whom, of course, came forward as close relatives of persons already in Canada and not because of their selection on any occupational basis.
More significant still, we brought forward in 1960, 1,583 newcomers who established themselves in their own businesses and provided employment for 6,189 individuals. The value of the businesses established by these newcomers is known to be in excess of $18i

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
million and down payments were made in connection with these businesses in excess of $9J million.
So far as agriculture is concerned, reports were received in 1960 of some 647 newcomers who had bought farms of their own, while 101 had rented agricultural land. Some 786 immigrant owners or operators became established in this manner and the total number of persons employed in these enterprises numbered 1,072. The value of the agricultural land involved amounted to $11.7 million and down payments on these purchases amounted to more than $4J million.
From what I have just said, Mr. Chairman, it will be evident that the immigrants who have come to Canada continue to show the initiative, industry and enterprise which enlarge and increase the employment opportunities, productive capacities and national wealth of this country.
What I have said with respect to our activities in this field during 1960 is, of course, only a continuation of what has been the continuing objective in the field of immigration over a long period of years. For example, in the past ten years 6,000 businesses have been established and 5,400 farms purchased by post-war newcomers to Canada. The value of these farms and businesses amounts to $140 million. It is conservatively estimated that they have provided employment for 35,000 persons.
It is well known that most immigrants are willing to work hard and sacrifice much in order to establish themselves securely in Canada. This is borne out by figures which indicate that they paid $69 million, or almost half the value of their businesses and farms, in cash down payments. This would indicate that not only do some immigrants-for example, United States citizens-bring substantial savings with them to Canada but also that immigrants are hard savers.
There has been a very marked upswing in the number of immigrants establishing businesses in the past two or three years. Roughly one quarter of the businesses established during the last ten years were bought in 1960.
There are certain patterns emerging from the statistics for business and farm settlements. In the business field just over 40 per cent of the settlements have been in Ontario, 30 per cent in British Columbia and 20 per cent in Quebec. Germans have established the largest number of businesses, followed by Dutch, British and Italians. The average immigrant makes his purchase from three to six years after his arrival in Canada.
In agriculture just over 50 per cent of the immigrant farmers favoured Ontario.
Next popular are British Columbia and Quebec. The average farmer spends five years working for someone else before buying his own property. Out of nearly 7,000 farms bought by immigrants over the last ten years, nearly 4,000 were in Ontario, just over 1,000 in British Columbia and 600 in Quebec. Dutch people bought two thirds of the farms and have brought experience, skill and new techniques to Canadian agriculture. The Canadian economy has been widened and strengthened by the influx of these new businessmen and farmers.
I should like now to make a brief reference to one of the special features of our activities in the immigration field during 1960, namely the special movements connected with world refugee year. During world refugee year, which officially ended on June 30, 1960, there was a most heartening response on the part of community groups, private and church organizations, and governments generally, to the special appeal launched under the leadership of the United Nations high commissioner for refugees. These efforts, many of them of a special nature, have continued throughout the period following the close of world refugee year, and the special facilities and arrangements made by the government through the immigration branch to encourage and foster this nation-wide response have been continued up to the present time and are being continued in suitable fashion.
During the 18 month period from the beginning of world refugee year to the end of 1960 more than 4,500 individuals were admitted to Canada under special refugee arrangements. The most notable feature of these arrangements was, of course, the special movements of tubercular refugees. The first of these movements, consisting of 100 selected t.b. cases, together with their dependents, entered Canada in the latter part of 1959 and the early part of 1960. A second movement, consisting of slightly more than 100 tubercular refugees and their dependents, came forward to Canada in the summer months of July and August.
Here I must pay tribute to the co-operation and help extended to the government by the various provincial governments and health departments throughout the country. These governments assumed the responsibility for the health and hospital care of the individuals brought forward and it is most reassuring to note that so far as the first two movements are concerned, well over two thirds of the t.b. refugees themselves had completed their active treatment and been discharged from hospital before the end of 1960. Only a relatively small number continued to require institutional care as of December 31 last.
1902	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
In consequence of these most encouraging results the government has recently announced, with the co-operation and consent of the provinces concerned, that it is prepared to admit a third group of tubercular refugees, together with their dependents, under the special arrangements which were established for the previous movements. The selection of this third group is now under way and it is expected that the movement will have been completed before the end of March, 1961.
I should like finally to say a word about the Immigration Act itself. It will be recalled that the speech from the throne referred to the expectation that a revised Immigration Act would be laid before parliament for consideration. Inquiries have been made from time to time as to when a draft bill is likely to be brought down. No one is more concerned about this than I am, and every effort has been directed toward the achievement of the desired objective of a full and complete revision of the act; but I am afraid there is very little I can add at this time to what I have said on previous occasions in reply to questions about the timing of this matter.
It will be appreciated, I am sure, that the timing of the presentation of any draft bill for consideration depends on a great number of factors which I am not in a position to predict at the moment. Chief among these is the general timetable for the business of the house and the progress of the government's legislative program as a whole.
Representations and inquiries have also been received in recent months from a number of important national organizations, notably the Canadian Welfare Council, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Labour Congress. Some of the representations received urged that more time be taken to complete the revision of the legislation and to make it possible for them to undertake a more complete and thorough study of the issues involved.
In connection I should like to repeat the assurances which I gave on this matter during the discussion of our estimates at the last session. The fullest opportunity will be given to all interested organizations to present their views on the general questions relating to immigration policy, and also on the form and content of the draft legislation itself.
The government will be only too glad to receive whatever help and advice these important and responsible organizations can give in order to ensure that the form and content of the legislation, when it is finally passed by parliament, will be as satisfactory as it is humanly possible to make it.

Mr. Chairman, like all other members of this house I was certainly very pleased to hear the report of the minister, especially in reference to the activities of the department and the government with respect to world refugee year. Of course, when the announcement was first made in the house it was received and acclaimed as indeed being an effort by the department to deal with the problems with what we like to refer to as the humane touch; the human touch, in fact. We certainly greet that with much pleasure and we are very glad to note that an announcement will be made that another group will be admitted very shortly.
Of course, dealing with hard core cases of immigrants is always a problem and the country is aware of it. It is certainly encouraging that the first effort has turned out very successfully, and this certainly augurs well for the treatment of further hard core cases whenever the humane touch requires it.
On the other hand, I was rather disappointed that the minister's report to the house seemed to be one purely of statistics. It was a statistical report as to how many came in from various places. Perhaps such a report should be made to the house in a statistical form, although we can get this information in the printed reports that reach our desks from the various departments. I had hoped that the minister would put a little of that humaneness into her report which the country had hoped would be ever present when she was summoned to that portfolio. The statistics she gave to the house, however, are completely devoid, apart from the question of world refugee year, of the humane touch which is required in dealing with human beings.
You could not have been listening to the speech.
I would like to say to the hon. member for Brome-
Brome-Missisquoi.

-Brome-Missisquoi, who has a reputation for being very erudite, that he should certainly know and remember the old adage that children should be seen and not heard, unless they are very wet; and the hon. member is very wet.
That is very smart; that is quite funny.
He will be here long after you have gone.

That, too, remains to be seen.
I do not know who undertakes to prophesy. You know the old saying "only fools prophesy". I am wondering whether members of the government are concerned because I

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
said that the minister-I may have touched her sensitivities, or theirs; I am sure I have not touched hers-
Oh.

I did not crown her with that glory which she probably expected to receive, because the country had hoped that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, as a woman, would bring a little more of that understanding, that family understanding, that motherly understanding, which I found was completely absent from her report.
The hon. lady's reference to the revision of the act was expected, but I am again disturbed by the fact that the minister has served notice that this revision may not come as soon as was expected. The country has been clamouring continuously for a revision of this act, and I think the time has come. The minister would certainly disappoint not only parliament but the whole country if a revision of the act is not brought down. It was mentioned on several occasions by the hon. lady during the last session. It was promised in the speech from the throne. Certainly we are expecting it. The minister has said that other organizations and people will have an opportunity to be heard, and that is true, but I am hoping that the hon. lady will also see to it that a parliamentary committee is appointed to study the proposed draft bill and that such a committee will be empowered to hear witnesses and receive representations from the various organizations in the country which might be interested.
All this certainly makes it clear that the minister and the government have not yet adopted a consistent policy with regard to immigration. I have been in rather close touch with immigration activities and it has been interesting to observe the minister's constant^ shifting from one position to another. Her juggling, her almost mercury-like policy with regard to immigration shows she is unable to keep her course steady in any shape, form or manner. It is a vacillating policy. The hon. lady sometimes takes one position and then, by order in council, she shifts that position and annuls the position she had taken.
During the past 12 months the minister has claimed she has been misquoted with regard to statements she is deemed to have made as to policy. She has blamed the press. She has blamed officials in her department, who are completely blameless, for errors in understanding her policy. She has been blaming others right and left.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened in patience to this, and I expect the hon. member to criticize me, but if he says
I have criticized members of my department I really must take exception to that remark.
I do not know whether to call it criticism but at one time the minister did make a statement that her policy was misunderstood because of officials in her department.
I never did.
That is pure punditry based on conjecture.

I am reading from an editorial which appeared in a very prominent paper in this country. It continues:
To the Italian community here and to many others, the obvious intent was a drastic curtailment of Italian immigration.
Of course, the minister faced a problem there and she quickly had to retrace her steps, which is not an easy thing to do. Some newspapers have said it was probably a very brave thing for the minister to have done. Let us see what the Toronto Daily Star said on April 23, 1959 under a big headline: "Mrs. Fairclough Retreats in Disorder":
That was an amazing performance by Hon. Ellen Fairclough in announcing the withdrawal of the order in council banning immigration of relatives of some Canadian residents. It was good riddance of a bad order. But Mrs. Fairclough's petulant tone and attempt to throw a smokescreen over the government's retreat made her sound like a little girl who had lost a piece of candy.

speechtext:
May I suggest the hon. member call it six o'clock?

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration AFTER RECESS
The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was talking about the vacillating government policy on immigration. Perhaps in modern language I could describe it in this way. The government seems to be playing its immigration policy by ear, meeting conditions as it sees them without having any fixed guide in its policy on immigration. If the government is playing it by ear I would consider it pitiable because the consequences are not reflected in any other tones than groans and anguish from heartaches and heartbreaks in preventing the linking together of broken families, and by increasing human sorrow. That is very clearly reflected in just a few headlines that I should like to read into the record. In the Toronto Telegram of April 3 we find the following:
Immigrant family curb aimed at limiting influx of Italians.
What year?

The year 1959. In the Globe and Mail of April 3, 1959, we find the following:
New curbs put on immigration for relatives.
In the issue of April 2, 1959, we find the following:
New immigration bar shocks city newcomers.
Again, the Globe and Mail of April 6, 1959:
Skill before kinship new immigration rule.
The Toronto Daily Star, April 3, 1959:
Sixty three thousand Italians hit by immigration cut.
Again, we have the Globe and Mail of June 23, 1960, with a smiling photograph of the minister with the following head note:
She deals in human beings counted in dry statistics.
This, Mr. Chairman, is how the country has been accepting this curb that is being placed on the linking together of families. As I said before, when a motherly woman was assigned to the portfolio it was generally hoped that she would bring to her office an understanding family touch and with benevolence she would help to unite separated families. In fact, when she first took office she declared that that would be one of her main objectives. We were hopeful, Mr. Chairman, but the hopeful were soon disillusioned when with almost Draconian rigidity she enforced the complex and confusing regulations and, unlike ministers before her, she did not often temper mercy with justice, as it was hoped she would.
During her almost four years in office the record shows that she did very little to modify the procedure to join families on the basis of relationship, age, or country of origin. I feel that after almost four years in office the minister should have something more to show in that regard. And now something new has been presented to us. Recently, a new requirement was apparently set up. This was announced by the minister in Guelph only a short while ago when she spoke of immigrants with skills. To make certain that I shall not misquote her, Mr. Chairman, I have her speech and I shall read from page 8 of the text that was provided. This is what she said:
We are doing a great disservice both to the immigrant and to our own community, when we bring to this country people who lack any kind of craft, skill or profession, who have no technical or other form of training suited to the demands of an increasing technical world.
If I were asked what I think is a real test of what makes a desirable immigrant, I think I should have to answer that it is a matter of what he has to contribute to Canadian progress and the strength and welfare of the Canadian community. At first blush that may sound like a selfish yardstick, but I am sure that if you give it a little careful thought you will agree that it is the only honest and sensible one.
No one will disagree very much with that, but will the minister tell the committee- and she has left the country unaware of this fact-whether this is now the top priority of immigration policy, or whether this is in addition to all the other complex problems which exist in the regulations? Does one replace the others, or are they to be dealt with together? In other words, must a person who now wants to immigrate to Canada fall into one of those complicated categories and in addition also be a skilled person?
I should like to illustrate it in another way. For example, can a Canadian citizen bring his father to Canada if his father is not a skilled worker, or can he bring his father to Canada only if he is a skilled worker? I hope the minister will clarify this. Surely it would be harsh to believe that the minister intends to place the importance or the emphasis on skills in preference to close relationship of relatives. Of course, I am of the opinion that it will simply complicate the situation.
Hon. members should be aware in detail of the complications which now exist in our immigration regulations. I have mentioned them on previous occasions and I should like to repeat them now. It is really an academic study so that all hon. members can understand and wrestle with the problem. The act sets out various types of citizens, or gives to different citizens different rights and privileges. I will give a few examples. Citizen A
[The Chairman.]

can bring certain relatives to Canada. Citizen B cannot bring people of the same relationship to Canada simply because they happen to live in another country, and when I speak of another country I am excluding countries behind the iron curtain. I am now speaking of other European or mid-eastern countries. Here is another illustration. Citizen A can bring to Canada certain relatives under certain conditions. Citizen B, who is equally a citizen, cannot bring to Canada people having the same relationship under any conditions. That too results from the fact that his relatives live in another country.
Here is another illustration. Citizen A can bring his parents to Canada regardless of their age. Citizen B, who is equal so far as citizenship is concerned, can only bring his parents to Canada if his father is over 65 and his mother is over 60. That too stems from the fact that they live in another country. Another illustration: Citizen A can bring a brother or a sister to Canada. Citizen B cannot bring a brother or sister simply because they happen to live in another country. Citizen A can bring his fiancee while Citizen B does not have the right to bring his fiancee to this country.
These are only some examples. There are many more similar complications and computations that one must conform with before one can really follow and understand a straightforward policy. Why should all citizens not have the same rights to bring their fathers or mothers to this country? Whether one lives in one country and another lives in another country, they are still fathers and mothers. Why should one citizen not be able to bring his father or mother to this country if they are not of a certain age? Are they different? Is their love or affection different? No.
All these, I say, are matters which require sound and careful study and analysis, and that is why the act should be revised.
While my hon. friend is pausing may I ask him a question?
If I will not lose any of the time allotted to me by allowing the question.

As I understand the rules,, you only have to sit down and you can get up and speak for another 30 minutes. Would my hon. friend tell me who was the instigator of these regulations against which he is railing and is it not true that they were instituted by the government of which he was a supporter until 1957?

I was hoping, in fact I was expecting that the minister would ask that question. We once discussed that point on a previous occasion. I said then that some
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration genius concocted all these combinations and computations which the minister certainly did not think were very nice at that time. However, she has been in office for four years and, having these complaints and knowing about them she is the only one who has been in a position to do anything about them. I have not given credit to whoever that genius was in years gone by. I do not necessarily have to accept or agree with what was done at that time because I am pleased to say that we on this side have no fear of saying that we disagree with a colleague. It may have been a good policy then and perhaps it was the work of a genius. He may have shown signs of genius at that time but the policy is outdated and outmoded. I blame the minister directly because she has been in a position to do something about the matter. I will put the argument this way. Since the minister has done nothing about it, perhaps she agrees with the genius who introduced these regulations.
I wonder whether the hon. member would answer a question.
I will only answer a question, Mr. Chairman, if I will be allowed 30 minutes from the time I sit down.
I was wondering, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that unless there is unanimous consent it is not possible to take into consideration the time used up by questions. Therefore, if the hon. member does not yield the floor, I will ask the hon. member for Bow River to resume his seat.
All right, ask the question.
Now that the hon. member has agreed to answer my question, I wonder whether he would identify this genius. Is it the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate?

I have not identified him. If the hon. member wants to do it, if he thinks he knows who it was, let him do it. I think the minister did it last year on one occasion. It was admitted. Nobody denied it. We recognize genius when we see it.
In the Liberal party?

Indeed, only in the Liberal party. I should like to draw something to the attention of the minister now that may surprise her a little. I refer to the question of a new policy. Is the minister aware, does she know, did she ever hear, do hon. members of the Conservative party know or are they aware of the immigration credo of their

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration own party laid down at a party convention? Let us see what that credo is. It is quite possible that very few of them have heard about it. I am now referring to Senate Hansard of April 4, 1960, page 498 and a speech made by a member of the other place. At that time this was said:
The Progressive Conservative convention, I notice, adopted the following resolution:
"Whereas a healthy and judicious immigration policy is necessary in order to provide a guaranteed market for Canada's vast natural resources and to reduce our vulnerability in the export market; whereas there are still thousands of refugees desirable as citizens who are not admissible to Canada under current immigration regulations; whereas this convention notes with satisfaction the efforts at the United Nations of Canada's minister of external affairs on behalf of refugees; that this national convention of the Progressive Conservative party recommend to the government-"
I ask members of the government to please note. I continue:
"-that the immigration regulations be amended, to enlarge the categories of admissible immigrants; to redefine the term 'refugee' so as to widen and extend the qualifications for admissibility under this category; consider and if deemed advisable increase and extend the existing facilities and personnel for the processing of immigrants in foreign countries."
Here is a credo on immigration that was approved by the Conservative convention and I ask the minister this question. What has her department done to implement any one of these orders, so to speak, contained in this resolution?
Now these tenets have in no way been implemented. They are noble tenets. I believe this is a good policy for immigration, and that is the program of the Conservative party. What have they done to implement any one of these provisions? For example, the resolution says that it failed to amend the act to enlarge the categories of admissible immigrants. Here, hon. members will note, is an order from the party to enlarge the categories of admissible immigrants. Did the minister do that? Did she do anything in that direction? No, she did nothing.
That is wrong.
The resolution calls for the definition of refugee to be redefined. Did the government redefine the meaning of the term "refugee" as instructed by its own convention? No, it did not.
The answer is yes.

Oh, there has been a modification of it, but not a redefinition. I asked the minister on the floor of this house if she would define now what "refugee" meant and her answer was, what the high commissioner for refugees says is a refugee we will acknowledge. It has never been otherwise.

There has been no change as she was instructed. The implications, as hon. members should know, are very wide if there were a redefinition of "refugee".
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the hon. member puts his question, I would mention that the time of the hon. member has expired. If the committee is willing to give unanimous consent, he may continue.
Agreed.

He is talking about the directions of a political convention to the government. I wonder if he would let the house know if the Liberals have put in their platform all the directions of the recent Liberal convention, and the resolutions that were passed there?

Is that not typical of hon. gentlemen shying away from their own responsibilities? They say that we did not do it and because the other fellow fails to do it, they should not do it. Surely the hon. gentleman who just asked the question knows as well as I do that the mere fact the other fellow does not do what he should do is no reason for me not to do it. I want to say that I know of nothing in the Liberal platform which will not be implemented as soon as the Liberal party has the power and authority to do so, which I hope will not be very long.
Then there is a third plank in the Conservative platform. This resolution instructs or authorizes the government to increase and extend the existing facilities and personnel for the processing of immigrants in foreign countries.
From what are you reading?
From the very same document that I read before.
What is it?
I will repeat it. Will the hon. gentleman please note it. It is a page out of the Senate Hansard for April 4, 1960, which is quite recent.
From whose speech?

I think it was Senator Cairine Wilson. She was quoting a resolution right out of the records of the Conservative party. Surely hon. members opposite should know whether or not there is such a resolution.
They do not know; they were never published.

Of course they were never published. They do not know, and it is obvious from their behaviour they do not know.
I should like to get to the third point. This is a direct instruction or authorization to the government and to the minister. She was authorized and instructed by her own party to extend the existing facilities and personnel for the processing of immigrants in foreign countries. Those of us who are in communication with immigrants constantly hear the government say, we have no facilities in that country. This may be so; it is quite possible. The government says, we cannot deal with this immigrant because we have no facilities for processing. Surely when instructions are given to remedy that situation the minister is in default and is failing to do her duty as minister of immigration when she does not remedy the situation. As a consequence, the whole country suffers.
I should like to point out too that I am one of those who believe in an active immigration policy. As the committee well knows I have been propagating that for the last 11 years. Like the minister herself, I believe that immigrants make jobs and immigrants do not take away jobs from Canadians. On a number of occasions the minister has very eloquently and very forcefully told the country that the immigrants who come to this country are a blessing. They create jobs; they create industry; they encourage work. I believe as the minister does. But what does the record show? The record shows a pitiful reduction in immigration in the last three or four years. In fact, we were told today that 104,000 immigrants came in during the past year. I have not in front of me the figures to indicate how many immigrants left Canada, but I feel sure if you were to strike a balance there would certainly not be a very great net gain for our country.
I have the feeling that if the government were to implement an immigration program- I know the minister is in some difficulty now. She is on the eve of revising the Immigration Act. I believe this is one of the finest things that the minister can do for her department, her officials and the country. I feel I have had some training in the law, but by no stretch of the imagination could I set down clearly what the policy of the immigration department is now. The officials of this department are eminently able, well experienced men, and desirous as they are of being of assistance they come up against confusion in this act which the minister should eliminate once and for all.
I am beginning to be sceptical of whether the minister is serious about revising the act. As I said, the revision was promised last year
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration and it was promised in the speech from the throne. I hope the minister is not waiting until the end of the session to try to rush it through or, alternatively, to say that there is not sufficient time to do so. Tonight she did say that it will depend upon the business of the house as to whether we will be able to have the act revised. Everything will depend upon circumstances. I say to the minister that she will be delinquent in her responsibilities if she does not introduce a revision of this act, have a parliamentary committee appointed to study it and give that committee authority to summon witnesses and hear representations.
Surely the minister is aware of the fact that the country is clamouring for the overhaul of this act. I should like to quote from an article in the Montreal Star of January 4, 1960, which is headed, "Time for an Overhaul".
Without delay, the Immigration Act should be reviewed and the operations of the immigration department surveyed. Either, if not both, is in need of liberalization. Arbitrary behaviour on the part of department personnel would lead one to think sometimes that they are constitutionally hostile to immigration. It is a question whether they should have the power of discretion they sometimes exercise.
I could quote any number of newspaper authorities who are urging the overhauling of the Immigration Act. As I said before, I think there should be an overhauling or revising of this act that would really place the entire policy into simple language, not complicated language, and would set it out clearly so that everybody with intelligence, would be able to understand it. If this were done it would relieve the country and it would certainly relieve the department. I speak for the officials of the department who I know are anxious to do their duty completely and thoroughly but who are sometimes hamstrung by the difficulty of understanding the language of the act.

speechtext: Shall item 51 carry?
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is seriously thought that the most important item in the estimates of the immigration branch would be carried without any reply by the hon. lady to the indictment made by the hon. member for Cartier, not merely of the current practice but of some of the regulations that have been in existence for quite some time and some of the practices that have been in existence for quite some time and which, in some cases, are anachronistic today. I may say that I was minister for about the same length of time or perhaps a little bit longer as the hon. lady has been in office. However, I changed the regulations
1908	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration or caused them to be changed or persuaded my colleagues to have them changed four or five times during that period. I must say that my attitude has been a sort of mixture of feeling flattered that the hon. lady considered my regulations to be so good that she has not been able to change them at all significantly and of feeling that they ought in some respects to have been changed in order to meet changing conditions. That has been my attitude to them.
In extenuation of my own conduct may I say this, and I am not going to defend it more. Nearly all of the instances given by the hon. member for Cartier-and he would perhaps recall this if I went further.-were cases in which liberalizations of the regulations were made and not cases in which restrictions were made. The hon. gentlemen did not point out that the reason that the parents of Canadian citizens can only be applied for when the father is over 65 years of age and the mother is over 60 years of age is that in those cases they are iron curtain countries and as long as the government sees fit-and this is not the fault of the immigration department; this was a decision that was made by the previous government and is presumably being carried on by the present government-and as long as the government feels that in the state of the world as it is at the present time it is necessary to have some security screen of immigrants and as long as it is impossible, as it is, to carry on security screening in countries behind the iron curtain it was felt that the highest considerations of the security of the state made it inadvisable to relax the regulations more than that.
Whether that is suitable to conditions in 1961, as we felt it was the only thing that it was proper to do at the time when I was minister, I should not like to express an offhand opinion. But that is the reason and the sole reason why there is a difference between, say, the parents of a Canadian citizen who happens to be living in a country behind the iron curtain and those who do not. I think perhaps that consideration ought to be put on the record.
I must say that it seems to me that the fundamental criticism that one could make at the present time of the state of our immigration to this country is this, and the hon. member for Cartier put his finger on it when, during his remarks he said he wondered whether there had been very much net gain in population in Canada in the last year or two from immigration. We do not have statistics, and I do not see any practicable way of collecting statistics on the number of people who leave Canada to settle permanently somewhere else unless we turn this country


into a sort of police state, which is not something I would like to see. I would not like to see us starting to ask every Canadian or every resident of Canada who leaves Canada questions such as these; why are you leaving the country? Are you going to stay permanently or are you just going down to Florida? Or things of that sort.
In the first place, I think it would slow up border crossings to such a degree that we would be obliged to have an army of immigration officers instead of the number we now have. I must say that I am glad that we live in a country in which we can have a fairly open border and I am not a bit in favour of changing that situation just for the sake of collecting statistics.
But there is something we can tell from the statistics of immigration into the United States, into the United Kingdom and into one or two other countries that keep records, those being the principal ones. We know that a regrettably large number of residents of Canada have left this country in the last two or three years and that there has been a good deal of comment about that in the press. That has been particularly true in the case of the United Kingdom and Germany in the last couple of years.
But the root cause of that situation, of course, is not any failure of immigration policy or of immigration administration. The root causes of that situation is the unemployment situation with which we are faced. I quite agree with the hon. member for Cartier that if there were some way of keeping people alive indefinitely until they could get jobs it would be desirable to keep up a flow of immigration even when it was difficult to get employment. However, I administered the department and I must say that I do not believe the Canadian people would support such a policy. I do not believe it is a practical policy to encourage people to come to Canada, when those people have no employment and have no real chance of getting employment. From experience that I have had and from studying the experience that the government has had since that time I know that nothing does more to spoil the prospects of future immigration than to have a considerable number of people come to this country with high hopes of getting jobs, spend two or three months here without getting a job and then go back and inevitably blame this country for their experience. As is commonly known, people do not like to blame themselves. I do not think there is any single thing that did so much to discourage British immigration, and will continue to discourage it just as long as the present government is in office, as the brutal cancellation of the Arrow contract and all the consequences it had on the destruction of

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
that complex which had been built up in the Toronto area of industrial research and development which was just by the stroke of a pen in a fit of irritation by the Prime Minister ended on a Friday when these people were brutally thrown out of work.
That is absolutely ridiculous.
Yes, it was absolutely ridiculous and it was utterly irresponsible.
The hon. member's remarks are utterly ridiculous and irresponsible.
No better comment could be made upon it than that which has just been made by the Minister of National Defence.
The hon. member's remarks are ridiculous and irresponsible.
That comment was typical of the hon. gentleman who usually speaks first and thinks afterward, if at all.

Abuse will get the hon.
gentleman nowhere.

I say that as a practical matter it does seem to me that there cannot be any permanently productive immigration, in the sense of bringing people here who will stay here, who will be contented and who will add to the upbuilding of the country, unless we can maintain the growth of the country, which is not being done at the present time. That is the basic problem, and it is not something that can be blamed on the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, much less on the department. Having said that, there have been one or two other-
Tell us something about second-class babies.

The hon. gentleman may be a better authority on that subject than I would be. If the child is the father of the man, I would not be surprised if he is.
There is one aspect-
Are you talking about the Horners?

There is one aspect of this subject about which I asked a question early in the session and received no answer. I feel it ought to be pursued because we have been told by a distinguished member of the government, a fairly recent recruit to the government, that when this government came into office there was a profound change in the immigration policy of this country. I do not want to be unfair to the hon. gentleman, the Secretary of State-who is not in the committee at the moment, I regret to say-but I want to read a press dispatch and I intend to read it first from the Toronto Star and then
from La Presse, because I feel we should have both on the record as here were two reputable newspapermen writing in newspapers in both languages, reporting the same meeting and reporting it in virtually identical terms.
I think we are entitled to some serious explanation of this from the Secretary of State and also from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. The Secretary of State undertook in a by-election campaign in the county of Labelle last October to say this. This appears in the Toronto Star of October 18, 1960, and I read the part that is relevant:
Mr. Dorion maintained stepped-up immigration under the Liberals, particularly the 240,000 admitted in 1956-
The 240,000 admitted in 1956; of course, the Liberals were to blame for that.
-when there were 292,000 unemployed,-
I do not know where the hon. gentleman got that figure. He certainly did not get it from the bureau of statistics:
-was largely responsible for current unemployment.
That is a remarkable statement; but after all that is just a matter of opinion. I do not hold the government collectively responsible for that extraordinary opinion expressed by the Secretary of State. I go on:
He accused the Liberals of trying to "anglicize" French-Canada by bringing over more immigrants from the British Isles than from any other European country.
I ask the minister whether she thinks that is a very helpful way for any minister of the crown to be talking in any part of this country. Then he went on, and this is in quotation marks:
"They tried to eliminate the French-Canadians for the benefit of the English," he said.
Then he said this, and this is the part that the minister should answer for:
Prime Minister Diefenbaker, he added, had promptly closed the door on this immigration-
That is the English immigration:
-and was trying to offset the Liberal "angliciza-tion" by fostering immigration from Italy.
That is a statement made by a minister of the crown, as a member of the government, in support of an unsuccessful candidate for election to this house, regarding what the Prime Minister had done and what the hon. lady is administering. I just repeat it because-

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with some amazement to my hon. friend, but it is possible that he was not in the house when the hon. member for Belle-chasse disclaimed this and, as a matter of fact, stated-
1910	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration Mr. Pickersgill: As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to yield the floor. I was in the house when the hon. member for Bellechasse was very careful not to deny this. He did not deny it at all. If the hon. lady can find any denial of these words, she understands the English language and the French language better than I do, because the hon. gentleman did not deny it. He evaded the question and gave a long quotation from something Mr. Harris had said, which had nothing to do with the case at all; but he did not deny this.
It would be very hard for him to deny it, for two reasons; because it appeared not only in the Toronto Star but in practically the same language in La Presse, and there are at least two or three members of this house who were present on the occasion on which the hon. gentleman uttered these remarks and heard them.
You were not there.
I was not there, I never said I was.
