speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I have in front of me Hansard for November 18, 1960 and the English translation of the remarks made by the Secretary of State, read as follows:
Mr. Speaker, fortunately, I have here the exact text of my statement, and I find that the reports-
He did not have a text.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
If I may continue, Mr. Chairman:
-appearing in some newspapers are substantially at variance with what I said.
"Substantially", that is the word.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The minister's statement in this house with regard to the inaccuracy of the statement appearing in the press is to be accepted.

I have no doubt that reports in the newspapers were substantially at variance with the hon. gentleman's notes, but that has nothing to do with the case. Either the hon. gentleman denied using those words, or he did not; and there is no denial there of the words I have read. All the hon. gentleman did was say that some of the press reports were at variance with the notes he had. He did not say they were at variance with the things he said; he said they were at variance with the notes he had. We know he is not the only member of the treasury benches who finds that the things reported in the newspapers are at variance with the notes they have.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; there is no mention of the notes that he had. He said:
-are substantially at variance with what I said.
I accept that.

Why did you not take
it up when he was here?
I did take it up when he was here. Why is he not here, incidentally, where he ought to be?
Why weren't you here yesterday?
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Mr. Chairman, I am speaking on the point of order raised by the Minister of Veterans Affairs.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understand that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is speaking to the point of order raised by the house leader, and I cannot entertain more than one point of order at the same time.

Precisely, Mr. Chairman, I say that the Secretary of State did not deny the express words I read. All he said was that some of the press reports were at variance with what he had said, as the hon. gentleman has just read. That may well be; but that is not a denial that the words I read were the words he uttered. And, of course, it happens that those words were heard by several members who are in this chamber at this present moment.
If the hon. gentleman wants to come into the house and say that he did not say those words, I shall be obliged, under the rule, to accept his word. But up to now he has not done that.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I would like to have that clarified. The hon. member seems to be rambling a bit. The point of order I wish to raise is referred to by Beauchesne in paragraph 148 (3) where it is stated:
Reference to debates of the current session is discouraged even if such reference is not irrelevant, as it tends to reopen matters already decided.
Again subparagraph (2) of the same paragraph states:
It is irregular to reflect upon, argue against, or in any manner call in question, in debate, the past acts or proceedings of the house, on the obvious ground that, besides tending to revise discussion upon questions which have already been once decided-
And so on. I suggest this is what the hon. member has been doing. He has done it on two occasions. The first was in connection

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
with the Arrow, and this is the second occasion. The question was discussed in the house and decided, and I suggest we should act in accordance with this rule and try to get the hon. member back to order.

It has never been recognized that questions asked on the orders of the day are previous debates. The purpose of asking questions on the orders of the day or placing them on the order paper is precisely in order to get material for use in debate. Therefore this is not reopening a matter previously debated. I am not aware that there has been any debate previously this session about the Arrow, though I know there was a debate in another session.

Further to that point of order, since the hon. member has rambled on I would refer him to paragraph 157 (6) which states:
A member quoting a newspaper in debate was ruled out of order by the Deputy Speaker who said: "The rule is quite clear, that the quoting of a newspaper, an author or a book which reflects upon debate before the house, either directly or indirectly is entirely out of order, because members are here to give their own opinion and not to quote the opinion of others."
I suggest we ask the hon. member to carry on the debate instead of continuing to make the irrelevant observations he has been making.

If the hon. member has finished reading from Beauchesne perhaps we could get back to the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I can go on to corroborate what I am saying from this dispatch of La Presse of the same date. Perhaps the house would be a little quieter, because it is more difficult for me to do this in a language which is not my habitual language. If I might have the attention of the house, I shall read what La Presse has to say:
(Translation):
He said also that present unemployment is a heritage from the Liberals, because the former government admitted 240,000 immigrants in Canada in 1956, when we had 292,000 unemployed.
Mr. Dorion said Mr. Diefenbaker closed the door on that immigration, adding that the Liberals "wanted, by this immigration, to eliminate the French Canadians to the benefit of the English", while ...
(Text):
This is in quotation marks.
(Translation):
.. while under Mr. Diefenbaker, we admitted more Italians to the detriment of English immigration."
(Text):
I say, is it not quite remarkable that reputable correspondents of two of the leading newspapers in this country, one in
French and one in English, should have given the same account of this situation in almost exactly the same words? Would it not be remarkable if both of them had imagined these words and if those who were there and heard them had also imagined them? If that is what the Secretary of State-
You are very brave to attack him when he is not here.

Bring him here. I am not in the least concerned about that. Anyway I am not attacking him. The minister said the Prime Minister had changed the immigration policy, that he had stopped British immigration and increased Italian immigration to prevent the anglicization of our country which was being perpetrated by the Liberals and restore the balance. I asked the hon. lady a rhetorical question: is that true? But I am not going to press her for an answer because I know perfectly well it is not true.
Then why did you bring it up?

I will tell you why I brought it up. I did so because I think that kind of speech is a disgrace to this country. It is a disgrace for a minister of the crown to make this kind of cheap appeal and cheap misrepresentation calculated to promote disunity in other parts of Canada. I think it is an improper way to behave and when a performance of this kind comes to light it seems to me it should be denounced and a record of it should be kept as an example of what many hon. gentlemen opposite and their friends have done in this country ever since 1911, and the moment the Secretary of State appeared on that platform he began doing it all over again. I say we should stop this kind of talk about whether one kind of immigrant is better than another. The plain fact of the matter is that we know from our experience, having had immigrants from nearly every country in the world, that those immigrants from nearly every country in the world and their descendants have become good Canadians; just as good Canadians as the descendants of the original inhabitants of this country or the descendants of the French or the English. If we are going to have a united country the sooner we have a stop to that kind of thing the better. That is the only reason and the only excuse I have for bringing this up.
If the hon. member for Bellechasse, the Secretary of State, had, when I asked my question first, got up and said without equivocation that he had never made that statement I would have had to accept his answer and I would not have mentioned the subject again. But he did not say that. He used
1912	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration words which were calculated to give that impression, but he did not say that because the hon. gentleman knew it would not have been correct if he had. That is why I raised this matter. I have no apology whatever to make for bringing up this question and I hope this will put a stop to that kind of speech by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house.

It had not been my intention to reply in any detail to the observations made by the hon. member for Cartier but since I have been challenged to do so by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate perhaps I should say a few words.
The hon. member quoted from my speech in Guelph which was made available to him last week. I fail to understand why he cannot read what was written in that speech. He purported to tell this house that by saying Canada wanted skilled immigrants I had inferred that none but skilled workers would be admitted. As he very well knows, I denied that first press report and if he had read my speech he would have been able to ascertain for himself what the facts are. I did not say in my speech that relatives would not be admitted, and he should know that, too, if he had read the speech. I fail to understand the hon. member's motives in imputing to me statements other than those I did make.
In so far as his other remarks are concerned, when he accuses me of being inhuman and vacillating and, I think he said, playing the immigration policy by ear, I should like to say to him, that if by that he means that my ear is open to the pleas which are made to me he is right. I have pursued and tried to pursue a flexible policy in so far as immigration is concerned. I do not like the act; I have said so on many occasions, but I have also said that I am not going to bring into this house some half-baked instrument to take its place.
I might say that some of the organizations to which the hon. member belongs are amongst those who plead most frequently for special consideration and, as hon. members know, special consideration can only be given by order in council. I make no apology whatsoever for having used the instrument of order in council to accede to some of the heartbreaking pleas of some of my hon. friends own friends.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred to the fact that on a number of occasions he had altered the regulations-
Or asked to have them altered.

-or made some variation in their application, I take it. That has been done by this government also on a number of

occasions. We are not operating under exactly the same terms as those which he left to us when he left this office. I could name a number of regulations which have been altered somewhat or modified. To call one to mind, I am thinking of the elimination of the bond which had formerly been required by fiancees, usually Chinese fiancees.
In answer to my hon. friend from Cartier who said that there had been no new definition of refugees-he called it a modification -well, whether it was a modification or not may I say we had a warm letter of thanks from the Canadian Jewish congress expressing their deep appreciation of the steps which were taken to make it permissible for those persons who might be classified as economic refugees, not normally recognized by the high commissioner for refugees, to enter this country.
As I said a moment ago, I make no apologies for the changes which have been made. I make no apologies for the fact that I have tried to pursue a flexible policy. I do apologize for not having brought in a new act before now, but I can assure hon. members that there were circumstances completely beyond my control which have prevented my bringing it in before now.

Because I think there would be a very general interest in this question I wonder whether the hon. lady can tell us just precisely where the investigation into the Chinese question is at the present time?
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I cannot give a precise answer to that.
A progress report.

The investigation is proceeding; a number of Chinese have come forward and have given information by means of which we are in the process of regularizing their status. A few have already been regularized. Some of the others are awaiting further information, but we expect that we will be able to deal with their cases.
In so far as the prosecutions are concerned, of course, those come under my colleague the Minister of Justice. I might say, though, that I am a little disappointed that more of the Chinese have not taken advantage of the offer which has been made to them by means of which they might have come forward and given us the true circumstances of their entry and their true names, and thus have been in a position to pass on to their children their proper identity. I think it is a mistake for them not to do so, and I am sure that in the years to come those who do not will bitterly regret it. I do hope that even yet a great many of them will

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
come forward and establish themselves as bona fide immigrants and citizens of Canada.

I noticed from the statistics that the hon. lady gave us, and I also noticed this in the newspapers, that immigration from China was about half of what it was in 1959. Is the hon. lady now satisfied that all the people who are now coming are bona fide immigrants in the sense that they are the persons whom they represent themselves to be, and that the situation which was being investigated is now being completely cleared up so far as all the current cases in Hong Kong are concerned?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I can undertake to make any such statement. We hope that we have investigated and traced all of the current entrants to the places where we know they pretend to be. I think the very fact that immigration from China has been cut in half-and which I might say is the direct result of fewer applications, not of action on the part of this department-will indicate that those who are coming forward now are the ones that are sure of their own bona fides. I do not think that under the present circumstances someone would come forward who knew that he was deliberately misrepresenting himself. In fact, he would be a very brash individual indeed to do so.

The hon. lady took some credit to herself with regard to changing the regulations with respect to fiancees. I am not sure that I entirely approve of the change which was made but that is a matter of opinion. She knows the reason why the original provision was made. Those fiancees from China were all admitted when I was minister as a matter of grace and not under the regulations at all. But it did happen occasionally that the passion that had prompted the application did not survive the encounter, and sometimes there was no marriage. It seemed to me that in those circumstances it was only fair that they should have a return ticket so that they could get back, because I do not think it is beyond the hon. lady's imagination-and perhaps she does not even need to imagine it-that sometimes some people who alleged they were applying for fiancees were applying for women for some other purpose. Is the hon. lady quite satisfied that the people she is admitting now as fiancees really are all bona fide cases, and can she give any figure as to whether the number has increased or decreased in the last year?

I am very happy to inform my hon. friend that we have not had one Chinese fiancee come forward who has
not fulfilled the marriage contract subsequently and since the bond was removed. I wish I could say the same for the fiancees who come from all other countries. That was one of the grievances when we removed the bond. We felt it was an unjust condition directed against the Chinese when possibly the Chinese more than any others were observing the conditions of their entry. Consequently I am very glad to say there have been no culprits since the bond was removed.

I do not think there were many of the return tickets used even before, if the hon. lady will recall the figures.
In view of the discussion we have had so far, I think it might be useful if either now or later the hon. lady would give us a record of the respects, not in which the practice has been changed, but in which the actual regulations have been changed since the present government came into office, and what the nature of the changes was and what the effect of them has been. If it could be done right away it would be all the better.

I can give my hon. friend some. The regulations were amended to enable Canadian residents of Asian origin to sponsor admission of their spouses, children and parents. Previously such sponsors had to wait until they acquired Canadian citizenship. This change enabled the reunion of families who would otherwise have been separated for five years.
In some cases.

Well, having regard to the fact that I was accused earlier of separating families I think maybe I might stress the point that this was done specifically to reunite families.
Then there was the order in council which amended the regulations to provide for the landing under minister's permit of persons who marry Canadian citizens or residents. This was intended to provide a little more control over the admission of fiancees by providing, if necessary, for the removal from Canada without formality of those who did not marry. I am sure my hon. friend will remember cases when he was minister where one person would bring forward successive fiancees, none of whom ever actually entered into marriage with him.
Certainly not with me.

I meant with the applicant. I am sorry. I have mentioned already the elimination of the bonding requirement and I have already mentioned the amended definition of refugees. These are the ones that come immediately to mind. There are other minor changes that I could secure for my hon. friend but these are the ones that are the most prominent.
1914	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
Could the hon. lady say how many refugees were admitted to Canada during refugee year apart from those who were brought in under the government's scheme, so to speak, the tubercular ones?
In round figures about 4,500, including some 700 or more who came in under the tubercular refugee scheme.
How many is it contemplated are coming under the extension of the direct government sponsorship?
At the present time we have made arrangements for 114 in hospitals. With their families I cannot say exactly what the number will be but it will probably be about 450.
Can it be said that, practically speaking, all the tubercular people in the refugee camps in Europe who would be willing to migrate at all have now been taken care of?
We have altogether only 96 left that we know of who can be brought forward.

I think this has been one of the most humane and commendable things that has been done since the Hungarian situation and, as the minister knows, I have never failed to commend what the government has done in this matter. I know there were people who felt that there was quite a danger to the public health. Some quite eminent doctors who are friends of mine have said to me that there are various kinds of tuberculosis and we might start a new strain in this country. However, there does not seem to be any evidence that any harm has been done or that there has been any infection of anyone already here as the result of this movement, and it undoubtedly has changed the very lives of a lot of people in a way of which I think every Canadian who has contributed to it ought to be rather proud of having had some part. I must say I am very happy indeed to commend the government for having done this.

Mr. Chairman, much as I should like to take all the commendation myself I must in all fairness pay tribute to the provincial governments who in their turn participated in this scheme by making hospital beds available and by entering into arrangements with the federal authorities for the care of these people. I think we can truly say that this has been a Canadian scheme which touched all classes and kinds of people because in addition to the part played in the scheme by the provincial governments a number of these people were brought forward by individuals, by groups of individuals and by


organizations such as churches and service clubs. Altogether I think it has been a mosi heart-warming effort.
I should like to make a few observations but I see the hon. member for Kootenay West rising.
I was simply going to ask a question. I do not want to interrupt the hon. member's line of thought.

I was really going on to make some observations about a different subject. I gather from what the minister has said about the revision of the Immigration Act that it is very far indeed from being in a final form for submission to the house. Therefore it may be that the minister would be interested in having my views as to some changes and improvements that I think should be made in the act. I would be very glad to mention a few of them.
The reason I am doing so right now is that the question of tuberculosis is one of them. I think that certain of the prohibitions now in the act should be removed. I could do a Pontius Pilate act over this because when the act was before parliament I was not a member of the house although the hon. lady was, so I had no direct responsibility whatsoever for what is in the act. When that prohibition was put in the act there were justifiable fears about contagion that are no longer justified at all. I know that I came pretty close to breaking the law on a good many occasions when I was the minister by actually admitting people to this country who, strictly speaking, were not admissible because they still had a spot on a lung that some doctor certified might still be active. I did not do it very often and, of course, I never landed them as immigrants.
I do not need to tell the minister that painful situations of this sort arise all the time because the law itself in my opinion is quite unnecessarily harsh. I do think that not only that particular prohibition but all the other prohibitions including the one about insanity should be examined. I feel very keenly about the one regarding insanity. As every hon. member knows, there are many kinds of mental disorder, particularly those kinds which young people have from which they recover and which make them no more prone to mental disease in the future than someone who has never had any mental disease. I think that the prohibition in that field is utterly out of accord with what would now be the public view of what would be appropriate. I would hope that there would be some relaxation in that field as well.
I also hope that the minister, though she certainly is under no obligation to do so, will

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
carry out the pledge that I made to the welfare association that if I ever introduced amendments to the act I would take out the provision for the deportation of persons who become public charges. I think that is a relic of the old days when the municipalities had to bear the whole burden in the case of any person who went on relief and they were unwilling to do so. But now that we have unemployment assistance, half of which is contributed by the federal treasury, for all kinds of Canadians and which applies not merely to unemployed persons but to everyone who is on relief for any reason, I certainly see no earthly reason why that provision should be there.
I am now going to embark on a subject which is much more difficult and about which I have done a lot of reflecting since I ceased being the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You have had more time.
As the Minister of Veterans Affairs has pointed out, I have had a little more time, and I have had to find other means of occupying my time that were more lucrative than just thinking.
You had better edit that statement.

Than just thinking? Perhaps with the permission of the hon. lady and of the house I might look at it and edit it to the extent that I think is necessary.
To come back to my point, one of the most difficult things was this whole problem of adjudication of deportation cases. When I was the minister I had the governor in council set up an appeal board in respect of the deportation of landed immigrants who I felt had rights. From the time I set up that board every landed immigrant was asked to opt- I do not know whether the minister follows this course-whether he wanted his case settled finally by the board or by the minister. Of course, under the law, the minister has to settle it. There is no escape because parliament has said so. If the person said, I want it settled by the board, then I did not alter the board's decision. If the person said, I want it settled by the minister, then I asked for the board's advice and while I generally followed it I felt I was under an obligation to exercise a certain measure of judgment myself. I think this course was quite legal, and I was advised it was quite legal.
However I would much rather have had a board that had the final jurisdiction and, if necessary, an appeal to the courts. I do not believe such a right of appeal to the courts would have been exercised very often. I have the view that once we accept a person as a
90205-6-121
landed immigrant he has certain rights. It is true he has not the same rights a Canadian citizen has but he has broken his ties with another country and we have said, you look like a likely citizen. We have accepted him and we have, therefore, incurred some kind of obligation.
I think it would be very much better to have these cases adjudicated by a tribunal. It would make the life of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a good deal more tolerable if she had no power to deal with these cases at all, just as she has no power to deal with citizenship cases. I do not believe the minister differs with me in the view that the amount of discretion that can be exercised should be reduced to the minimum.
The only reason there is any discretion under the act-at least in my experience during the whole time I administered it-is so that it can be exercised for the benefit of the applicant. I have never known discretion to be exercised the other way. In fact, I do not believe it could be exercised the other way. Either a person is legally admissible or he is a borderline case, and if you admit him you are exercising the discretion in his favour. The question is, do you want to retain any discretion of that sort. I think that unless we are going to have a quota system or a complete open door policy there has to be a measure of discretion exercised somewhere. I do not believe the Canadian people would ever accept the open door policy, and I am very much against a general quota system. I say this not as a final opinion, but I just offer this gratuitous advice to the minister and to her officials for consideration before the act is revised.
I have come to the conclusion that on balance there ought to be a provision in the act for the establishment of an appeal board to consider any appeals in sponsorship cases. This is a very difficult task for a minister. A minister is under all kinds of pressure from all kinds of people, some of them benevolent and some of them quite mercenary. It does seem to me that if we could lay down rules for sponsorship and then create an independent tribunal to consider any cases that were appealed by the legal sponsor in Canada, it would make this portfolio supportable. I must say I have a good deal of sympathy for whoever has this task at the present time because there are too many decisions that nobody but the minister has the right under the law to make for one human being to be expected to make them, to be able to make them conscientiously and live a normal life. I speak rather feelingly about this. I tried to administer the act exceedingly conscientiously, perhaps too conscientiously. At any rate I am
1916	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration honestly trying to make some suggestions which I think might make the law more tolerable from every point of view.
I must confess that in the case of applicants for admission to Canada who have no sponsors, who have no previous connection with Canada, I do not believe their cases are capable of being adjudicated by any kind of tribunal or board any better than they can be handled by the officials of the department. When it comes to a question of selecting from the outside world those people we want or do not want to be residents of Canada, who have no connection or relationship of any sort with this country, I do not think we should do anything which would confer a right upon other people. I do not believe that would work. I believe the moment you did it you would have the administrative machinery and the adjudicative machinery clogged with so many cases, most of them I am afraid I would have to say unworthy cases, the whole process would break down.
We have had some experience with those who have got into the courts. The hon. lady will remember a certain person by the name of George Christian Hanna who was of great help to her party in Vancouver in the general election of 1957. I think before she had ceased to hear about him she was as sick of his name as I was. It is true there are a number of undesirable people, and there is no earthly reason why we should have them in Canada. The notion that anyone who is not very welcome in his own country but who wants to come here should be able to come here is one that I do not believe the Canadian people would accept for one moment. I think a clear-cut distinction could be made. I say this after a lot of reflection about the difference between immigrants of that type and sponsored immigrants. This would, I believe, involve extending to the English and the French, who do not -have it now, the right to sponsorship which is given to other people. These people did not have it in my time because they were relatively freely admissible anyway. I think that would have to be modified.
There is one other matter which I suppose, in a sense, more properly comes under citizenship than under immigration, but is closely related to it. In view of the rather higher degree of literacy, the rather higher educational qualifications generally, and the greater need there is going to be in the future if we are to provide for good immigration and to make things agreeable to immigrants in Canada, I have been wondering if we should not give consideration to reducing the five-year waiting period for Canadian citizenship. At the present time I think it is really more attractive for most people


to stay in Europe than it is to come to Canada. I think we might give consideration to the question of whether five years is too long a period to wait for citizenship. I have not any fixed views on this subject but I think it is one that perhaps merits some consideration.
There is one other question and I come back to it because I omitted it earlier. There were also these other deportations. I suggest to the minister that she change the nomenclature in the act so that a clear distinction is drawn, by using a different word, between what you do with landed immigrants and what you do with people who are here as visitors. Much of the misunderstanding that exists at the present time about the administration of the act is due to the confusion in people's minds between the deportation of immigrants and the deportation of visitors.
I must say that on balance, having regard to all the circumstances, I think that some advisory body should have the capacity to review deportation orders of visitors as well. My own opinion is this; and may I say that I have an extremely high regard for the officers of the department. I do not think they have ever deserved much of the abuse that has been heaped upon them with regard to being inhuman bureaucrats and so on. That has not been my experience and it has not been the experience of most of my friends. But for all that, there is no doubt that when a decision is made by a single individual in Sydney and another one is made in Victoria, there is the possibility of a good deal of difference in the interpretation of the law. I think it would be a good thing if there were in existence some formal advisory body that would consider cases-and they would be relatively few

in which there was a desire for an appeal to the minister and give an opinion which could be made public, if necessary. Once this appeal is taken I think the information should be publishable. If the person does not want it published, he should not appeal. If he feels he has grounds for appeal, he should take the risks of publication. I think the minister understands thoroughly what I mean. Many of these visitors are deported for reasons to which they would not wish to have much publicity given.
I suggest that this procedure would also serve a useful purpose. But I say to the minister that if she can think of some other word it might be helpful. I do not care which one she calls deportation and which one she does not. On the whole I would use the word "deportation" for immigrants and 1 would get another word that had a different connotation for those people who are just visitors in the

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration
country and who have no right whatever to stay here if they are objectionable in any way.
These remarks were not very well organized. They are rather a wide-ranging expression of opinions but I hope they may be a little bit helpful in the drafting of legislation.

Just before my hon. friend asks his question I should like to thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and tell him that practically all of the suggestions he has made have been under consideration. I cannot find too much wrong with what he has said. If he has any other ideas on the subject I hope he will not hesitate to send them along to the department. Out of the wealth of his own experience in this branch I know that he must have some definite ideas, as he has just demonstrated.

I just wish to make a few observations on this item. First of all let me say I think all of us appreciate the extremely difficult task confronting the officials of the immigration branch because of the pressure from various groups to get people admitted and often pressure by members of parliament in contradiction sometimes to things they say in the House of Commons. I want to say publicly that in travelling through the country and in talking to a good number of persons, including some members of this House of Commons, I find that there is a general appreciation of the good work being undertaken by the present deputy minister and of his generally fair, sympathetic and humane approach.
In listening to the remarks of the hon. member from Bonavista-Twillingate who speaks with considerable experience I must say this, although it rather pains me at times to be compelled to agree with him. I must say that he put up a reasoned case with respect to various groups of immigrants, and particularly with respect to the admissibility of sponsored immigrants who are coming to relatives who will provide for them so that they are not going to be a public charge. I think his suggestions in that respect were quite sound.
On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, while I realize all the difficulties, it appears that we still have not a planned immigration policy in which we bring forward people on the whole when they can be absorbed into the economy without displacing Canadian workers or, shall I say, competing with Canadians for short housing and things of that sort. In the opinion of the members of this group who have always advocated a planned immigration policy, immigrants' applications should be processed in the country of origin and then they should be brought 90205-6-121i
forward as they can be fitted into the stream of employment satisfactorily in this country.
I want to say a word or two about landed immigrants. This matter has been a sore point with some members of this group and other members in this House of Commons. I refer to the abuse of this term "landed immigrants". The minister has had brought to her attention on a number of occasions where people come in from the United States, as they have done in British Columbia in recent years, as landed immigrants. I have had them tell me after they have arrived here that they have used the term "landed immigrants" only to come in and work for three months. They come in as landed immigrants not intending to stay as immigrants and take employment on that basis away from Canadian workers; they come in and work on pipe lines and things of that sort. I think there is considerable abuse of the opportunity to come into Canada as a landed immigrant. I think there should be some consideration of that term and I think that something should be done to make certain, as far as possible, that a person who comes to Canada as a landed immigrant is a genuine settler and intends to try to establish himself or herself in this country and intends to make a living here. We have had numerous cases of that kind in the interior of British Columbia, particularly in the building of pipe lines.
Then we have another abuse of the immigration facilities and in one case I found the officers of an international union cooperating with men in the United States, to the disadvantage of the Canadian workers, in making application for men to come into this country on the assumption that there was no Canadian capable of doing the job. They come in as technicians of a certain type and inside of a week they were driving a truck. I think that is a question that requires careful looking into and I think something should be done with respect to regulations in order to strengthen our officers at the ports of entry.
Then there is the question of securing employment for immigrants and I have raised this question previously. I think it is entirely wrong that, shall I say, the seeking of employment for Canadians and for immigrants should be in the hands of two departments. Here we have the employment service of Canada carrying on its functions normally with its officials largely tied to offices, with inability to travel. We have these officers dealing with registrations and applications of workers for employment in the region which the office serves, and we have the immigration officer doing his duty, able to travel all around the country. He
19X8	HOUSE OF
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration receives a wire to say there are 20 immigrants coming tomorrow, and one immigration officer told me this was a proper headache.
I know several instances where he has just happened to meet an employer who wanted a man in a small community in my constituency and who had not time to register at the national employment office at Nelson or Trail. The immigration officer said, "I have certain men coming at a certain time, I can provide you with men", and one or two, or a number of immigrants obtain employment within a day or two of arrival in Canada.
At the same time there are in that community men who have had applications in the employment office for six months, married men with children, veterans who fought for this country in the second world war particularly. I know of cases where there has been hard feeling among the Canadian citizens affected in this way.
It is also unfair to the immigrant, who is sometimes subjected to a kind of disfavour, to put it very politely indeed, in a small community because he walks into that village -I do not blame him-and takes a job which other men are seeking, because they have been unemployed for some period of time.
I do think consideration should be given to bringing this question of employment under the unemployment service of Canada so that they can place applicants, as they register for jobs, in positions which are vacant. If someones arrives rather late, there is provision made for these people to be cared for and looked after in other ways for a certain time. I think that would be better than having this unfortunate state of affairs that causes a considerable amount of annoyance, to say the least, at certain times.
I want to ask the minister, at the request of a number of my constituents, what happens to an immigrant who has not become a Canadian citizen and who has committed a criminal offence or offences and has been sentenced to penitentiary for two years or more. What happens in the case of an immigrant who is sentenced to a year in jail, or six months in jail? In a case brought to my attention in the city of Revelstoke an immigrant spent six months in jail on three occasions, and the chap came back and went to work, and so on. What is the policy of the department in respect to immigrants who commit crimes, who are not Canadian citizens and who obviously, from their records, are not suitable citizens? What does the department do upon their release from penitentiary?

Mr. Chairman, the usual practice is this. If a person who has not yet acquired domicile-which means residence, after being landed, for five years- commits an offence and is charged and sentenced, he then becomes liable to deportation. There is the odd case where, if he is a first offender, he might be given a chance to see whether he can make good. But his period of residence toward the establishment of domicile stops when he gets into trouble with the law, in most cases.
Do you mean by that he has to start his five years over again?

In the event that he has more than one conviction, of course in the average case he would be immediately deported. I might say, though-as my hon. friend probably knows-it is difficult to deport a person who comes from an iron curtain country, because the matter of deportation requires the consent of the country to which he will be deported. So I cannot give my hon. friend an over-all answer; but the general rule is that a person who has not yet acquired domicile and who has committed an offence for which he is convicted and serves a sentence would be deportable.
Would the minister mind commenting on my suggestion that this search for employment for both Canadian citizens and immigrants be brought under the Department of Labour.
Mr. Chairman, this is not at all a new suggestion. Not only my hon. friend but many other persons from time to time have made this suggestion.
Even Conservatives, when they were in opposition.

If the immigrant concerned comes from the United States or from some other English speaking country to an English community, or a French speaking country to a French community, he could orobably report to the local national employment service and take his chances with others who are making application. However, it must be borne in mind that the immigration department is responsible for these people, or has made itself responsible for them for a year after their arrival. Many of them require an interpreter at first. They certainly require to be told the conditions under which they would seek employment in this country. In other words, they need to be guided for a considerable length of time after they arrive in Canada.
These are just a few of the reasons why we consider it necessary to do what we can to assist them. Moreover, if they are not

employed they become more or less a charge on the immigration department. Consequently we do what we can to assist them to find housing, to find employment and to generally guide them in their first days in this country.
It is not our intention at any time to take work away from Canadians. In fact we have bent over backwards in that regard. The remarks which I made indicating the manner in which we are proceeding to try to circumvent such circumstances are the very remarks for which I was roundly criticized in this house today and in some of the newspapers of the country. But that is the very reason why we believe we should only bring into the country such workmen as have skills which are required at the present time and for which there are vacancies.
I might draw to the attention of my hon. friend that it is quite possible-I have said this on other occasions-that in a certain line of work there may be vacancies in the city of Toronto and surplus workers in Vancouver. The surplus workers in Vancouver, particularly if they are family people, are very loath to pull up stakes and go following the call of a job in the city of Toronto; and vice versa. We have these situations all the time.
So regardless of the fact that there may be unemployment in the country, there are always vacancies which are crying to be filled in some parts of the country. We do our best not to cause any difficulties in this regard, and we certainly try not to take jobs away from Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, could I just ask the minister one more question. I have been very patient indeed today, because I have been absent a great deal of the time. Has the minister given consideration to doing something to strengthen this section that permits immigrants to come in as landed immigrants when it is obvious that they are coming in under false pretences? It happens repeatedly. I want to explain this to the minister. I thought she was a bit snippy with me the other day when I asked a question, but I have forgiven her that already. I must say that this was brought to my attention and I suggested that the R.C.M.P. should check on this matter.
This is what I did. There were half a dozen men who came across from the United States at either Paterson or Newgate in my constituency, the ports along the Kootenay border. These men had come in as landed immigrants. I got in touch with the R.C.M.P. and told them these men claimed to be landed immigrants. They had come in as settlers and were working on the pipe line. I told the R.C.M.P. that it had been brought to my
Supply-Citizenship and Immigration attention by other employees that they were boasting of the fact that they were only going to work while the pipe line was being constructed and then they were going back to the United States.
I had the R.C.M.P. check their licences. They were staying in British Columbia and using their United States licences because they were claiming to be only visitors. My suggestion was that the R.C.M.P. should check some of these cases. If they found a man had come in and was still using his United States licence under the pretext that he was a visitor on the one hand, in order to avoid taking out a British Columbia licence, claiming exemption as a visitor for six months and was claiming to be a landed immigrant on the other hand, there would be clear proof that there had been an entry under false pretences. I made that suggestion then, and now I make it again seriously. I think a few checks might do something to stop this practice which is very annoying for Canadian workers looking for employment on the same jobs.

I find it a little difficult to understand the situation, because these people who come in as landed immigrants must, after all, undergo a certain examination, a health examination, and so on. I do not see any number of them doing that for the sake of being here for three months. On the other hand, if they come in as landed immigrants I think their automobiles would be listed as part of their household goods. I do not know what the regulations may be in British Columbia but in other provinces they are not allowed to use their cars after a stated period of time before securing a licence so I think it would be fairly easy to check. If a person comes in as an immigrant and brings his car as household goods, surely the provincial licensing authorities would be hot on his trail to make sure he lives up to his obligations. We have from time to time checked the reports which have come to us with respect to visitors working, particularly on pipe lines and on this one project at Cranbrook spread-is that the one the hon. gentleman was referring to?
That is right. That is the most recent one.
Just recently we checked that and there were only eight men working on it who were in the category of landed immigrants. All the others were Canadians.

The minister mentioned
Cranbrook spread and I notice that the leader of the official opposition made a speech in Cranbrook quite recently, touring around having certain designs in view, and

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration one of the things brought to his attention at that meeting was this very matter, and I understand there were some vehement complaints made. There may have been only eight landed immigrants working at the time the minister made her check, but there were many more than that. In my district the number went up to hundreds when the pipe line was being built from Penticton to the southern portion of British Columbia. Incidentally the contractor refused to hire men through the national employment service. The manager told me the United States contractor told him he was not going to be bothered by this potty national employment service, but said: I am going to bring in the men I need, and the rest will line up outside the office door so I can pick the ones I want. One group was put to work for a week or two and then that group was fired and a new group was taken on, and so on. It was most unsatisfactory.

We have a complete report on this, and if the hon. gentleman wishes to pursue the matter further we shall be glad to give it to him.
On the general question, I would remind the hon. member that it is one thing to ascertain what a person does and quite another to ascertain his intentions. All these people come forward as landed immigrants and fulfil the requirements of the act and bring their household goods. I do not know how we could possibly say to some of them: you are obviously not landed immigrants and obviously you do not want to stay in Canada. If it were obvious, we would not let them in.

I wish to ask a short question. Are any immigrants landing in this country from behind the iron curtain, and are there many inquiries from people living behind the iron curtain about immigration to this country?

Only from those who have relatives in Canada. We get inquiries from persons who have relatives behind the iron curtain in various countries who would like to bring their relatives to Canada. We get such inquiries from time to time. I would not say the volume is great, but we get quite a few.
The hon. member also asked whether there had been any immigrants landed from any countries behind the iron curtain.
Oh yes, there have been.

This is a subject I should like to pursue a little further. There have been periods, as the hon. lady well knows,

when in certain of these iron curtain countries there may be a temporary relaxation and it would be somewhat easier for Canadian citizens who had left relatives there to get, say, their parents out of those countries. At the time I ceased to be minister that was certainly true of Poland. That was just after the troubles of 1956. A great many people managed to get out at that time. There have been one or two periods when it has been possible for a few people to get out of Russia but not very many. I understand there have been one or two cases where parents have even been allowed out of Hungary, but I am not sure if that is correct. I wonder if the hon. lady has any statistical information and if she could indicate what the prospects are and also what procedure has to be followed.

I am afraid I cannot describe the procedure in sufficient detail at this time to be useful, but in answer to an earlier question, I now have the figures. Last year 4,426 persons came in from a number of iron curtain countries.
May I ask a factual question? Does that include Yugoslavia?
Yes.
Of course, there are two views about whether Yugoslavia is an iron curtain country and that is why I asked that question. Does that number also include people from China?

No. There were 881 from Yugoslavia. Poland has from time to time permitted persons to leave; not all who wished to, but most of them come forward. When there are indications that a certain country is relaxing its procedures with regard to permitting its nationals to leave we try to hurry visas for those persons who have waited, probably for a long time, so that they may rejoin their people in this country. It is a spasmodic thing. Sometimes a country will permit persons to leave, and then, all of a sudden, close the gates and allow none out. These are situations which again require some flexibility in the policy of the government.
Progress reported.

reading of that bill will pass the house fairly quickly; also in view of the fact that it is our intention to move that following second reading the bill be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs where the clauses may be studied in detail. That will be followed by the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
On Thursday, I generally attempt to forecast the following week's business, which is subject to change, but next week it will be this: on Monday we will have a private members' day; Tuesday will be government business with these items called, No. 9 on today's order paper, a resolution in the name of the Minister of Transport dealing with a proposed railway to Mattagami lake in the province of Quebec. The second item on Tuesday would be No. 3 on today's order paper, the second reading of Bill No. S-3, to repeal certain laws relating to the signal station at Halifax. If there were any spare time on Tuesday we would then take up item No. 7 on today's order paper, the motion to set up a select committee on research.
For Wednesday, the first item to be called would be item No. 11 on today's order paper,
Business of the House
referring the report of the Canada council to the public accounts committee.
